Eversmann’s giant robber-fly is a large predatory fly included in the 2006 national edition with the historical category III / LR-nt. The book gives a body length of 38–50 mm and a forewing length of up to 26 mm. The body is slender and covered with a grey bloom; the thorax is massive, the eyes are large and protruding, and the legs are long, with hairs and bristles. The elongated proboscis and transparent wings form part of the description of its appearance, but a photograph is no substitute for identification by morphological features. GBIF accepts the exact binomial Satanas gigas; a discrepancy in the year of authorship between the book and the Backbone is noted in the research report.

The national account lists records from the Talas, Chatkal and Uzun-Akhmat valleys, the Chüy Valley, the western part of the Issyk-Kul basin and other areas. Its habitats are described as virgin steppe, wasteland and sparse scrub on hills and in the foothills up to 1900 m. Adults and larvae feed on other insects; the account names locusts and horseflies as prey. The larvae develop in soil or decaying wood. The adult flies are on the wing from late June to mid-September. Ploughing of steppe tracts and the use of insecticides are named as the main limiting factors. For its protection the authors propose studying its distribution and ecology, and then creating micro-reserves free from ploughing and insecticide treatment. Whether these proposals have since been implemented, and the total population size in Kyrgyzstan, have not been established.
A slender fly 38–50 mm long with a grey bloom, a massive thorax, large protruding eyes, long hairy legs and transparent wings.
Adults fly from late June to mid-September. The larvae develop in soil or decaying wood; this information is given in the national account.
Both adult robber-flies and larvae are predators that feed on other insects. The account mentions the Moroccan locust and horseflies among the prey of adult flies.
The 2006 account describes development as taking one year; the larvae live in soil or decaying wood. Details of egg-laying are not given in the material used.
Historical records are listed for the Talas, Chatkal, Uzun-Akhmat and Chüy valleys, the western part of the Issyk-Kul basin, the Inner Tien Shan and the Fergana fringe. No new points are created.
Virgin steppe, wasteland and sparse scrub on hills and in the foothills, up to 1900 m according to the national account.

Korzhinski’s pear is a wild fruit tree whose national account gives the Chatkal and Fergana Ranges of Kyrgyzstan. In the 2006 edition the species was assigned the historical national category VU. This is a separate classification: the global IUCN category does not replace the national one and comes with its own source. According to the description, the tree reaches 10–12 m and has a rounded, spreading or elongated crown, dark brown shoots and elongated leaves with serrated margins. The flowers are white; the fruits are broadly pear-shaped, greenish-yellow, juicy and slightly astringent. These features help in getting to know the plant but are no substitute for checking herbarium material.

Its habitats are described as dry, gravelly, stony and fine-soiled slopes and the banks of mountain streams in the lower and middle mountain belts at altitudes of 1200–1700 m. The plant reproduces by seed and by root suckers. According to the account, in the wild it flowers in May and fruits in late August to September. The book stresses the value of the species for breeding drought-resistant cultivars. The felling of fruit-bearing trees and the lack of regeneration from seed are named as the main limiting factors. The historical source reports cultivation in the botanical garden of the National Academy of Sciences of the Kyrgyz Republic from seed collected on the Fergana Range; the present-day outcome of this work has not been separately verified. The authors recommend monitoring the state of the species and protecting all known trees. No dated quantitative estimate for the entire wild population of Kyrgyzstan has been found, so its numbers remain unknown.
A tree up to 10–12 m tall with a spreading or elongated crown, elongated serrated leaves, white flowers and greenish-yellow pear-shaped fruits.
Dry, gravelly, stony and fine-soiled slopes and the banks of mountain streams in the lower and middle mountain belts, at altitudes of 1200–1700 m according to the national account.
Reproduces by seed and by root suckers. According to the 2006 account, in the wild it flowers in May and fruits in late August to September.
In Kyrgyzstan, the Chatkal and Fergana Ranges, according to the 2006 edition. Up-to-date administrative evidence and locality points require separate verification.
Dry gravelly, gravelly-stony and fine-soiled slopes and the banks of mountain streams; lower and middle mountain belts, 1200–1700 m.

The cinereous vulture is a bird given its own species account in the second edition of the Red Data Book of the Kyrgyz Republic. The historical national classification gives category VI and the designation NT. The current international category is shown separately, based on an exactly matched record in the IUCN dataset. The national account describes nesting within Kyrgyzstan and links its habitats to the subalpine and alpine belts of the Tien Shan. In the south of the country, observations at lower altitudes are also given. The generalised distribution information does not represent new geographical points and does not prove that the bird is present in all areas today.

The book describes the species as resident. It builds its nests in trees, most often in juniper, and less often on cliffs. Branches are used for construction, and the nest cup is lined with the wool of mountain goats and domestic sheep. Early laying is described: the first eggs appear in February–March, and the clutch usually consists of a single egg. According to the account, the chicks hatch in April–May and fledge in August–September. Records of birds over carrion and near concentrations of ungulates show a link with food resources but give no quantitative description of the diet. The decline of wild ungulates and shooting are named as adverse factors. Recommended protective measures include locating and protecting nesting sites, creating mini-reserves and studying its breeding biology. The historical observations are not turned into an estimate of present-day total numbers. Whether the proposed measures have been implemented, and the current population, require separate research.

The national account describes it as a resident species of the subalpine and alpine belts; it has been observed in mixed flocks with the Himalayan griffon. Nests are placed in trees, most often in juniper, and less often on cliffs.

The account describes a bird observed over a horse carcass and recommends using the carcasses of domestic livestock at special feeding sites. The detailed quantitative composition of the diet has not been established.
According to the 2006 account, the first eggs are laid in February–March, usually one egg. The chicks hatch in April–May and become capable of flight in August–September.

Nesting is described within Kyrgyzstan, mainly in the mountain belts of the Tien Shan; individual observations are given for the southern middle mountains. Up-to-date points require separate verification.
The subalpine and alpine belts of the Tien Shan where wild ungulates live and domestic animals gather; individual observations are described below these belts.

The Egyptian vulture is a migratory scavenging bird included in the historical national Red Data Book with the category V / VU: R. The Russian account deals with the species Neophron percnopterus and specifies that the nominate subspecies occurs in Kyrgyzstan. Species rank is retained here: the international assessment refers to the exactly matched species and is not borrowed from another subspecies. The national source describes Kyrgyzstan as the north-eastern edge of the overall range. Its main habitats are desert foothills and middle mountains with highly dissected relief; the bird visits the subalpine belt less often. It prefers open areas and may occur in cultivated landscapes.

The account calls the Egyptian vulture a useful scavenger. Nests are built on cliffs or on raised artificial structures of old buildings; dry twigs, wool and other materials are used in their construction. A clutch of two eggs is described, and both parents take part in caring for the young. This information is not a new observation but a retelling of a historical scientific source. A shrinking food supply resulting from the decline of wild ungulates, together with shooting, is named as the main threat. The authors recommend locating nesting sites, preventing disturbance during the breeding season, establishing mini-reserves and working with local people. Cooperation with ornithologists in the countries where the species winters is also proposed, to protect it during breeding, on passage and in its wintering grounds. The existence of these recommendations does not confirm that they have been carried out. Individual old observations are kept in the research notes but are not published as a present-day estimate of numbers in Kyrgyzstan.
A migratory scavenger of open foothill and mid-mountain areas. The account notes a link with cultivated landscapes and occasional visits to the subalpine belt.
The national account characterises the species as a scavenger; the decline of wild ungulates is linked to a shrinking food supply. The detailed composition of the diet is not given.
Builds its nests on cliffs or on raised artificial structures of old buildings. The account reports two eggs and both parents taking part in caring for the clutch and brood.
According to the 2006 account, Kyrgyzstan lies on the north-eastern edge of the range. Historical observations are given for northern and southern parts of the country; no new points are added.
Desert foothills and middle mountains with sharply dissected relief, mainly open areas; less often the subalpine belt.

Regel’s eminium is a low-growing perennial described in the Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan as a rare member of the flora of the Western Tien Shan. Its underground tuber is flattened and spherical, and its light green leaves grow at the base. Its most striking feature is the dark, velvety spathe surrounding the spadix. The small flowers lack a perianth; female and male flowers occupy different parts of the same inflorescence.

The plant is associated with the foothills and the lower mountain belt, above all with loess soils. The national article names the Fergana, Chatkal and At-Oinok Ranges; the overall range also includes the Northern Pamir-Alay. It flowers in April and May. Reproduction by seed is stated, but the fruiting period and information on cultivation are not given.

The conversion of foothills to rain-fed farming and excessive early-spring grazing are named as the main threats. The authors proposed protecting its habitats, monitoring its populations and introducing the plant into a botanical garden. A qualitative statement that it is rare is no substitute for a population count. This information dates from the 2006 edition, and its present-day status needs to be checked.

The plant is 20–40 cm tall; the flattened tuber is up to 3 cm thick. The leaves are basal, oblong or oblong-lanceolate. The spathe, 8–18 cm long, is velvety and blackish-violet inside. The spadix ends in a club-shaped appendage 5–9 cm long.

The national description associates the plant with loess soils, and less often with fine-soiled and gravelly soils, in the foothills and the lower belt. Conversion of these areas and the use of pastures in early spring are named as factors in the loss of its habitats.
It flowers in April–May. The source states that it reproduces by seed but gives no fruiting period; there is no information on pollinators.

The historical national source gives the foothills and the lower belt of the Fergana, Chatkal and At-Oinok Ranges. The overall range is described as the Western Tien Shan and the Northern Pamir-Alay. Present-day occurrence points have not been confirmed.
Loess soils, and less often fine-soiled and gravelly soils, of the foothills and the lower mountain belt; according to the 2006 description.

In the national Red Data Book, Zenaida’s foxtail lily is presented as endemic to the Fergana and Alay Ranges. It is a herbaceous plant with a short growing season and underground organs that include a rhizome and thickened roots. The hairless stem reaches 50–80 cm. The broadly linear leaves are gathered in a rosette and have a channelled surface and a glaucous colour. The flowers are distinguished by the combination of a violet-brown back to the perianth segments and very pale, almost white margins.

The species is described from fine-soiled and gravelly slopes of the lower and middle mountain belts. It flowers in June and fruits in July. The fruit is a smooth, spherical capsule. The available article contains no quantitative population counts, no information on cultivation and no detailed description of how it reproduces.

The main threats are linked to economic activity where it grows: spring grazing, the picking of flowers and the digging up of rhizomes. In 2006 the authors considered that no specific conservation measures had been developed and recommended botanical reserves together with monitoring. The national category VU refers specifically to this historical edition; its current legal position and the condition of its localities require separate verification.

The stem is hairless and 50–80 cm tall; the thickened roots are 6–7 mm thick. The outer leaves are 6–30 mm wide, glaucous, keeled and channelled. The perianth segments are about 10 mm long, with a violet-brown back and almost white margins; the capsule is smooth, spherical and 7–8 mm wide.

A geophyte with a short growing season in the lower and middle mountain belts. The source describes fine-soiled and gravelly slopes; its precise requirements for moisture and soil composition have not been measured.
According to the 2006 edition, it flowers in June and fruits in July. No information is given on pollination, germination or vegetative reproduction.
The national article names the Fergana and Alay Ranges. The description of the range is historical, with no confirmed present-day coordinates.
Fine-soiled and gravelly slopes of the lower and middle mountain belts.

Zoya’s yellow desert candle is a yellow-flowered plant that the 2006 Red Data Book describes as a narrow endemic of the Kyrgyz Range. Its hairless stem reaches 25–40 cm, making it noticeably shorter than many other foxtail lilies. Narrow, pointed leaves are combined with a cylindrical, many-flowered inflorescence. The perianth segments form a bell-shaped flower with prominent veins; after flowering a smooth, spherical capsule develops.

The species is described from gypsum-bearing slopes of the lower mountain belt. Its short season of development includes flowering in April–May and fruiting in May. The article gives no data on numbers or cultivation. The Russian and English descriptions differ in the individual gorges they list, so only the geography that both agree on, at the level of the range, is retained here.

The authors regard spring grazing, the picking of flowers and the digging up of rhizomes as the main threats. Botanical reserves and monitoring of the state of populations are recommended; the materials used contain no confirmation that these measures have been carried out in the present day. The historical category VU and national listing are not evidence of current numbers or of legal status in 2026.

A hairless stem 25–40 cm tall. Linear, pointed leaves 5–6 mm wide. The inflorescence is cylindrical and many-flowered; the bracts, 1.5–2 cm long, are longer than the flower stalks. The yellow bell-shaped flowers have a perianth 15–16 mm long with prominent veins.
A perennial with a short growing season on gypsum-bearing slopes of the lower belt of the Kyrgyz Range. The national description gives no quantitative data on its dependence on soil conditions.
Flowers in April–May and fruits in May. No detailed information on reproduction or pollinators is given.

Both language versions of the national article associate the species with the Kyrgyz Range. The list of gorges differs between the versions and is not carried into the draft as confirmed precise geography.
Gypsum-bearing slopes of the lower mountain belt of the Kyrgyz Range.

In the national description, the twelve-dentate onion is presented as a narrow endemic of the Chatkal Range. It is a perennial geophyte with a small rounded bulb and a tall, ribbed stem. Its two flat, narrow leaves have rough margins. At the top of the stem is a dense inflorescence, roughly hemispherical or spherical in shape. The pinkish-violet flowers are star-shaped; after flowering the perianth segments bend back and twist.

Unlike species of open high-mountain meadows, this onion is described among shrubs and on forest edges in the middle mountain belt. It flowers and fruits in May and June. The national article contains no population count, no information on cultivation and no details of pollination. The population size therefore cannot be judged from the mere fact that the plant is listed in the Red Data Book.

The 2006 source reports that the species is protected in the Sary-Chelek Nature Reserve. The authors additionally recommended botanical reserves, monitoring and restrictions on bulb digging and grazing. Use as spring pasture, the picking of flowers and the removal of underground organs are named as threats. This historical information does not confirm its present protection status; the category VU is retained with an explicit reference to the edition.

A single rounded bulb 8–10, sometimes 12 mm in diameter; the stem is 60–80 cm tall. Two flat leaves 2.5–6 mm wide. The dense, many-flowered umbel is hemispherical or almost round, and the flowers are pinkish-violet. The stamen filaments are two-toothed and ciliate at the base.

A perennial bulbous geophyte of scrub thickets and forest edges in the middle mountain belt. The national source notes the destruction of plants through collecting and damage to the places where it grows through grazing.
In the national description, flowering and fruiting are dated to May–June. Pollinators, germination conditions and methods of vegetative reproduction are not described.
In the 2006 edition the range is given as lying within the Chatkal Range; the Sary-Chelek Nature Reserve is mentioned. No present-day records or coordinates have been added.
Scrub thickets and forest edges in the middle mountain belt.

Semenov’s onion is distinguished by its golden-yellow perianth, which later turns reddish. The Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan describes it as a perennial bulbous plant of the Inner and Central Tien Shan. Its cylindrical, relatively poorly defined bulbs sit on a rhizome. The stems are short, up to 40 cm, with smooth leaf sheaths. The two or three broadly linear leaves are flat and channelled, and the dense, head-like inflorescence resembles a ball or an egg.

The species’ habitats are linked to the high-mountain belt: alpine meadows, saddles and turf-covered slopes facing north and west. It flowers in June–July and fruits in August. These periods are known, but its mode of reproduction, numbers and the results of cultivation are not described in the article used.

The authors single out spring grazing, the picking of flowers and the digging up of bulbs as risk factors. In 2006 no specific conservation measures were considered to have been developed; botanical reserves, monitoring and restrictions on the removal of plants were proposed. The historical national category VU is not carried over into the global IUCN status field. Its present-day distribution and the effectiveness of protection have yet to be verified independently.

The stem is 10–40 cm tall. The cylindrical bulbs are up to 1 cm thick, with brownish, almost net-like tunics. Two to three leaves 5–15 mm wide; the inflorescence is head-like and spherical to ovoid. The bell-shaped perianth segments, 10–15 mm long, are golden-yellow and later turn red.
A geophyte of high-mountain alpine meadows. Saddles and turf-covered slopes facing west and north are named as its habitats; specific altitudes and soil measurements are not given.
Flowers in June–July and fruits in August. The national source does not establish its mode of reproduction; the presence of bulbs does not in itself confirm vegetative reproduction.
The national article gives the Inner and Central Tien Shan. This is a historical description of the range, without confirmation of present-day occurrence points.
Alpine meadows of the high-mountain belt, saddles and turf-covered slopes facing west and north.

The national Red Data Book describes Knorring’s larkspur as a rare relict species with a fragmented range in Kyrgyzstan. The stems reach 35–45 cm and are covered in spreading hairs on their lower part. The leaves are concentrated near the base; their blades are divided into five segments, which are further cut into lobes. The upper part of the stem branches and bears two to four flowers on very long pedicels. A characteristic feature of the flower is its slender cylindrical spur, forked at the tip.

The source gives the northern slope of the At-Oinok Range, the northern spurs of the Turkestan Range and the northern macroslope of the Alay Range. The plant grows on mountain slopes and rocks of the lower and middle belts. It flowers in June and reproduces by seed; information on fruiting times and cultivation is lacking.

The main limiting factor in the article is unregulated grazing that puts excessive pressure on pastures. No special protection measures had been developed by 2006, and the authors recommended assessing the state of populations across the whole range. The description “very rare” has not been turned into a numerical estimate. The VU category remains a historical national assessment, and the species’ present-day status needs to be checked.

Stems 35–45 cm, with spreading hairs below. Leaves on long petioles, palmately divided into five segments, each cut into three lobes. Two to four flowers on long pedicels; spur slender, cylindrical, forked at the tip. Nectaries and staminodes pale violet.
Mountain slopes and rocks of the lower and middle belts. The source describes the range as disjunct; the impact of excessive grazing is named as the main risk factor.
Flowers in June and reproduces by seed. Fruiting, pollinators and germination conditions are not given in the national article.

According to the national description: the northern slope of the At-Oinok Range, the northern spurs of the Turkestan Range and the northern macroslope of the Alay Range. No new observation points have been added.
Mountain slopes and rocks of the lower and middle mountain belts.

The juniper horntail is a large hymenopteran whose life cycle is tied to juniper wood. In the national description the female reaches 20–40 mm excluding the ovipositor and has a wingspan of 40–52 mm; the male is noticeably smaller. The black body is combined with yellow or reddish-yellow areas. Females have a long ovipositor, which they use to lay eggs in wood.

In Kyrgyzstan the species is described from juniper forests of the lower and middle belts at altitudes of 1200–2300 m. The national article lists the Chatkal, Fergana, Turkestan and Alay ranges. The larvae colonise severely weakened, dying and freshly felled trees, as well as stumps. The authors consider a report of larval development in poplar to be mistaken.

The source reports one generation a year, with adults active in summer and autumn, the timing varying between altitudinal zones. The main conservation task is to preserve juniper stands and areas with weakened and dead trees. Historically its habitats were protected in the Sary-Chelek and Besh-Aral nature reserves and in Kyrgyz-Ata park. Category III, LR-nt reflects the 2006 national assessment, not the current global IUCN status.

Female 20–40 mm long excluding the ovipositor, wingspan 40–52 mm; the male is about one and a half times smaller. Body black with yellow or red-and-yellow areas. In the female the antennae and legs are reddish yellow and the wings rufous yellow; in the male the wings are greyish and darkened.

Larval habitats are severely weakened, dying and freshly felled junipers Juniperus semiglobosa, J. turkestanica and J. seravschanica, as well as stumps. According to the 2006 article, flight in the lower zone begins at the end of June and lasts until September; in the middle zone it runs from the end of July to October.

The national source links the larvae to juniper wood and describes galleries filled with bore dust. Details of diet and adult feeding have not been established; the source explicitly rejects development in poplar.

The national article gives one generation a year. Females lay eggs in the afternoon in sunny, windless weather, mainly on the shaded side of the trunk. Clutches of two to three eggs lie at a depth of 10–14 mm; the embryonic stage lasts 12–15 days.

Historically recorded in the Besh-Aral and Sary-Chelek nature reserves, on the northern slopes of the Turkestan and Alay ranges, in the Kyrgyz-Ata Gorge and in the northern part of the Fergana Range. This is the 2006 list, without confirmation of present-day occurrence.
Lower and middle belts of juniper forest, 1200–2300 m above sea level.

Kuznetzov’s longicorn wasp is a small black-and-yellow wasp with marked differences between the sexes. Males stand out for their especially long antennae with a long club; in females the antennae are noticeably shorter. The national description gives a body length of 10.5–12 mm and a wingspan of 20–22.5 mm. The plant-based diet of its larvae sets this wasp apart from the usual idea of wasps as predators: the offspring receive a mixture of nectar and pollen that the female carries in her crop.

The species occupies dry patches of mountain slopes and clay bluffs, from the tree-and-shrub belt up to subalpine meadows, at altitudes of 1800–3100 m. The book gives scattered records from the Talas, Alay and Terskey areas, and some of the Issyk-Kul records require the synonymy to be checked. Adults are found from June to August, nests are made in light loess-like soil, and one generation a year is reported.

Overgrazing, ploughing, land reclamation and insecticides are named as potential threats, along with natural enemies and the isolation of populations. The authors proposed micro-reserves with regulated use of pastures and hay meadows, and further study of the species’ biology. The historical category III, LR-nt has not been transferred to the global IUCN field.

Body length 10.5–12 mm, wingspan 20–22.5 mm. Black with a yellow pattern; wings yellowish, darkened at the tip. Female antennae short, clubbed, 12-segmented; in the male they are comparable in length to the forewing and have a long club.

Lives in places with a dry microclimate, open slopes and clay bluffs. Adults are found from mid-June to the end of August. According to observations in the national article, males are especially active around midday, and females usually settle briefly nearby before entering the nest.

The larvae are fed a mixture of nectar and pollen carried by the female in her crop. The source notes visits to Sympegma regelii, Dracocephalum integrifolium, D. stamineum and plants of the genus Thymus; the exact share of each food source is unknown.
Builds nest burrows in the soil, preferring light, loess-like soil. The national article gives one generation a year. Clutch size and the length of larval development are not given.

The national article gives scattered records for the Talas and Alay ranges. The Terskey and southern Issyk-Kul records depend on an assumed synonymy with M. tianshanicus and require independent verification; they are not used as new confirmed records.
Dry, desert-like and steppe-like mountain sites with open slopes or clay bluffs; altitudes of 1800–3100 m in the historical description.

The national record for the desert monitor refers to the subspecies Varanus griseus caspius, and this rank has been kept in the draft. A species-level photograph not identified as caspius does not substitute for an image of the correct taxon. The book describes the Transcaspian desert monitor as a diurnal predator of the deserts and semi-deserts around the Fergana Valley, active from April to October. It shelters in enlarged burrows of rodents, birds and tortoises, as well as in burrows of its own up to three metres long.

Its food includes small vertebrates, eggs and invertebrates. Females lay six to twenty eggs in June or early July; in the national description incubation lasts up to three months. The geography in the book includes old records in the foothill zone around the Fergana Valley and a few dated reports, which are not used as present-day observations. The size of the population remains unknown.

The main threats are agricultural development of semi-deserts, the expansion of settlements, mining and persecution of the animal. The authors recommended a special reserve, control of capture and the development of captive breeding. The Russian article and the English summary give different threat categories, so the single category field has been left blank. The information in the book on bans and international lists is historical and does not confirm the legal provisions in force in 2026.

A diurnal predator, active from April to October according to the national description. It enlarges the burrows of other animals and digs its own, up to 3 m long. The source notes a decline in suitable desert and semi-desert habitats; a sighting in an unusual shrubland habitat has not been turned into a typical preference.

According to the 2006 article, it feeds on rodents, lizards, birds, tortoises, snakes and their eggs, insects and other invertebrates. The old book’s claim about toxic saliva requires separate present-day verification and has not been included in the scientific description.

National article: sexual maturity in the third year, a clutch of 6–20 eggs in June to early July, incubation of up to three months. After hatching, the young go into hibernation and appear above ground the following spring; local present-day data are lacking.

The historical national article links the subspecies above all with the foothills around the Fergana Valley. Old mentions of the Chüy and Talas valleys do not confirm its present occurrence. Reports from 1985, 1992 and 2005 are kept in the original source but have not been turned into new map points.
Deserts, semi-deserts and adyr foothills around the Fergana Valley; the historical range of the subspecies caspius.

The black grouse is a large, sedentary bird of typical gamebird appearance, with marked differences between the sexes. The national article keeps the species-level record Lyrurus tetrix and separately notes the Tien Shan subspecies mongolicus. The subspecies has not been added as a separate candidate. In Kyrgyzstan the species is described from the spruce forests of Chong-Kemin and the eastern part of the Issyk-Kul basin, where a shrubby understorey alternates with open glades.

Breeding is linked to spring leks: in April–May the males gather on scrubby slopes and perform their courtship displays. Males take no part in incubation or in caring for the young; the usual clutch in the source is seven to nine eggs. The diet includes insects, the leaves and seeds of herbs, fruits and berries; in winter the book mentions conifer needles.

Grazing in the spruce forest zone and poaching are named as threats. The source reports historical protection in the Karakol and Chong-Kemin national parks. A dated transect observation from 2003 is kept separately: it does not allow the numbers for the whole country or the current trend to be estimated. The national category VI, with the designation Near Threatened: R, belongs to the 2006 edition. The photograph of a European black grouse illustrates the species but does not identify the local subspecies.

The national article describes the black grouse as a large bird of typical gamebird appearance with well-marked sexual dimorphism. Sizes and a detailed diagnostic description of the plumage are not given in this article.

A sedentary bird of mountain spruce forests with an understorey of rowan, barberry and other shrubs, alternating with glades. In the breeding season the males form leks on scrubby south-facing slopes.

According to the national article, it feeds on insects, the leaves and seeds of herbs, fruits and berries; in winter, on conifer needles. Age-related differences in diet and the proportions of different foods are not given.

Lekking takes place in April–May; males are polygamous and take no part in incubation or rearing the young. Females reach sexual maturity by the end of their first year. According to the source, the usual clutch is 7–9 eggs.

Historically recorded in Kyrgyzstan in the spruce forests of Chong-Kemin and the eastern part of the Issyk-Kul basin. The national text assigns these populations to the subspecies mongolicus; present-day occurrence has not been updated.
Mountain spruce forests with a shrubby understorey, interspersed with open glades.

The whooper swan is a large waterbird with white adult plumage and a yellow-and-black bill. Its general appearance is confirmed by the university reference Animal Diversity Web, while the information on Kyrgyzstan is taken separately from the national Red Data Book. The 2006 edition describes it as a rare breeding species that is common on migration and in winter. Historical reports of nesting on Son-Kul do not confirm that this continues today.

The whooper swan uses the shallows of large water bodies rich in submerged vegetation. Sedge beds are noted at the former nesting sites on Son-Kul, and the shallows of Issyk-Kul as wintering grounds. According to the national article its diet is plant-based: aquatic and shoreline plants. Sexual maturity is given as the fourth year of life, the clutch contains up to seven eggs, and both parents care for the young.

Severe frosts and ice forming over the feeding shallows can cause wintering birds to starve. Poaching is also named as a threat. The authors recommended strengthening the protection of wintering sites, creating a protected area on the western shore of Son-Kul and carrying out regular monitoring. Old seasonal bird counts have not been carried over into overall numbers. Category VII, LC belongs to the historical national assessment.

Adults are white with black legs; the base of the bill is yellow and the tip black. Young birds are greyish brown, with a pinkish bill and a black tip. These species-wide features are given according to Animal Diversity Web, without a separate diagnosis of the Kyrgyz populations.

In the national description it is common on seasonal migration and in winter. It uses shallows rich in vegetation; the freezing of feeding areas on Issyk-Kul in severe frosts is named as a cause of winter starvation.
According to the national article, it feeds on aquatic and shoreline plants. The composition of the diet by plant species and the seasonal proportions of foods are not given.

In the 2006 book, sexual maturity comes in the fourth year of life and the clutch contains up to seven eggs. Extensive shallows with emergent vegetation are used for nesting. Both parents raise the cygnets. Present-day nesting in Kyrgyzstan has not been confirmed.
Historical nesting on Son-Kul, passage over the country’s large water bodies, and wintering on Issyk-Kul. Current nesting sites and new observations have not been added.
Shallows of large water bodies with submerged and emergent vegetation; historical wintering sites in the shallows of Issyk-Kul.

The ferruginous duck is a diving duck; the adult male has reddish-brown plumage and a white iris. The female is duller and has brown eyes; the white undertail coverts and white wing bar are important for identification. These features are confirmed by the scientific encyclopaedia of the National Museum of Natural Sciences in Spain. They help to distinguish the species from similar pochards, but identifying hybrid birds requires a specialist.

The 2006 Red Data Book describes passage through the Chüy Valley, the Issyk-Kul area and the syrt lakes of the Inner Tien Shan. Birds arrive in spring in April, and autumn migration takes place in September–October. In summer, moulting birds were found on high-mountain lakes. The diet is dominated by parts of aquatic plants and seeds; aquatic invertebrates and small fish are recorded less often.

The growing recreational and economic pressure on the water bodies used for feeding and moulting is named as the main threat. The authors recommended targeted conservation measures, public education and regular counts of birds on passage. Possible nesting in northern Kyrgyzstan was discussed as a line of enquiry, not an established fact. Seasonal flock sizes have not been turned into a national population figure; category VI, NT keeps its historical reference.

The male in breeding plumage is reddish brown with a white iris; the female is duller and less rufous, with a brown iris. Both sexes have white undertail coverts and a white wing bar. The museum reference warns that young and hybrid birds are difficult to identify.

A migratory species. According to the national book, the first birds appear in spring in April, and autumn migration takes place in September–October. Moulting birds have been recorded on high-mountain lakes in summer. For resting and feeding it prefers water bodies with rich aquatic vegetation.

The national source lists the vegetative parts of aquatic plants and seeds, and less often caddisflies and their larvae, molluscs and small fish. References to particular food families have not been turned into quantitative shares of the diet.

Historically on passage in the Chüy Valley, the Issyk-Kul area and on the syrt lakes of the Inner Tien Shan, including Son-Kul and Chatyr-Kul. The national article treats local nesting only as possible.
Lakes, reservoirs and ponds with rich aquatic vegetation and small aquatic animals.

The red-breasted merganser is a diving duck with a long, slender bill whose edges help it to hold on to fish. The university reference describes marked differences between the sexes: the male in breeding plumage has a dark green head, a white collar and a speckled breast. These general features of appearance are kept separate from the national information on distribution. The 2006 Red Data Book links nesting in Kyrgyzstan to the Issyk-Kul basin, above all the eastern part of the lake.

Nests are built on the ground in shoreline thickets and lined with down. The national text gives nesting in May–June and clutches of eight to ten eggs. Combined broods with a single female are sometimes seen, but the authors do not consider the reasons for this to have been fully established. The diet includes small fish and aquatic invertebrates.

The main threat named is drowning in fishing nets while diving. The destruction of shoreline vegetation and disturbance can also harm the birds. The book recommends a seasonal restriction on net fishing in Tyup Bay, monitoring and counts. An estimate of ten to fifteen breeding pairs has no year attached and has not been carried over into the numbers field. Category VII, LC is historical, and present-day nesting needs to be verified.

According to Animal Diversity Web, body length is 51–64 cm; the bill is long and slender with serrated edges. The male in breeding plumage has a dark green head, a white collar, a speckled breast and grey flanks. Species-wide features do not replace local observations.

The national article describes nesting in shoreline shrubs and suggests that a large proportion of the birds winter on Issyk-Kul. The birds dive for food, which makes them vulnerable to nets; the presumed year-round residence has not been declared established for all individuals.
According to the national book, it feeds on small fish and aquatic invertebrates. The proportions of foods and particular prey species are not given.

According to the national source, nesting takes place in May–June. Nests are on the ground among shoreline vegetation and lined with down; the clutch is 8–10 eggs. Combined broods have been recorded, but their origin is not established in the article.
In the 2006 edition it is recorded in Kyrgyzstan in the Issyk-Kul basin; surviving nesting was linked to the east of the lake. Present-day occurrence and nesting sites have not been updated.
Water bodies with shoreline shrubs and vegetation in which ground nests can be hidden.

The white-headed duck is a diving duck recognisable by the appearance of the male: a white head with a dark cap and a blue bill with a swollen base. The female has a darker facial pattern. Its general appearance, diet and breeding are confirmed by the university reference Animal Diversity Web; this information does not prove nesting in Kyrgyzstan. The national Red Data Book describes the white-headed duck in the country as a rare passage migrant.

On migration the bird may stop on water bodies with reeds and bulrushes. The historical article discusses the Chüy, Issyk-Kul and Fergana valleys. The species-wide diet includes the larvae of aquatic insects and the seeds of aquatic plants. For breeding populations the reference gives clutches of four to nine eggs and incubation of about twenty-two to twenty-four days; local breeding data are lacking.

The deterioration of aquatic habitats, the burning of reeds, fishing and hunting are named as threats in the national source. The authors recommended restricting spring hunting at possible passage sites. Large numbers of migrating white-headed ducks cited in the old article without a clearly defined area have not been attributed to Kyrgyzstan’s population. Category IV, EN reflects the 2006 edition; present-day legal restrictions and the global assessment have not been established here.

The male has a white head with a black cap and a blue bill, broadened at the base; the female has a whitish face with a dark cap and a stripe across the cheek. The body is chestnut brown, 43–48 cm long according to Animal Diversity Web.

Historically a rare passage migrant in Kyrgyzstan, resting on water bodies in spring and autumn. The species-wide university reference describes diving as its way of obtaining food. Nesting in the country is not claimed.

According to Animal Diversity Web, important foods are chironomid larvae and the seeds of aquatic plants; crustaceans and the green parts of plants are also eaten. This is species-wide information, not an analysis of diet in Kyrgyzstan.

The species-wide reference gives clutches of 4–9 eggs and incubation of 22–24 days. The data refer to breeding populations elsewhere in the range; the national source does not confirm nesting in Kyrgyzstan.

The national article describes rare passage through water bodies of the Issyk-Kul, Chüy and Fergana valleys. Assumptions based on sightings in neighbouring Kazakhstan have not been turned into new confirmed local observations.
On passage, water bodies with shores overgrown with reeds and bulrushes; reservoirs have also been recorded historically.

The black-throated loon is a waterbird whose national assessment in the 2006 Red Data Book stresses the danger that local nesting will disappear. In breeding plumage the species has a grey head and hindneck, a black throat with white stripes on the sides and a black back with a white pattern. These species-wide features are confirmed by Animal Diversity Web. The national text assigns Kyrgyz birds to the nominate subspecies, but the draft keeps the species rank Gavia arctica.

Historical nesting is described in the Tyup and Jergalan bays of Issyk-Kul. The book states plainly that there were no confirmed population figures for that time and that it was doubtful whether nesting continued; in winter the birds could be found across the whole lake. Fish and aquatic invertebrates are the food given. The article dates sexual maturity to the age of three, the start of nesting to mid-April and the usual clutch as two eggs.

Drowning in fishing nets and the destruction of habitats are named as threats. The authors recommended establishing the state of the population and restricting net fishing where the birds concentrate. An old figure for breeding pairs has no survey year and is kept separately. Category III, CR: R belongs to the historical national assessment, not to the global status of the species.

In breeding plumage the head and hindneck are grey; the throat is black with white vertical stripes on the sides. The back is black with white spots and lines. The description, from Animal Diversity Web, is species-wide; winter plumage is not described separately.

The national book distinguishes former nesting on Issyk-Kul from winter sightings. The lack of confirmed nesting in the book has not been treated as proof that the species has disappeared from the country altogether.
According to the national article, it feeds on fish and aquatic invertebrates. Prey sizes and the proportions of diet components are not given.

In the national description, sexual maturity comes in the third year, nesting begins in mid-April and the usual clutch is two eggs. This is the source’s biological account; current nesting in Kyrgyzstan has not been confirmed.

Historically, Issyk-Kul is given for Kyrgyzstan: former nesting in the Tyup and Jergalan bays and possible winter sightings across the whole lake. No new points or present-day nesting have been added.
The large lake Issyk-Kul; historical nesting sites in the Tyup and Jergalan bays, with other parts of the lake used in winter.

The white stork is included in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan under the name Ciconia ciconia. The account links it with foothill and lowland river valleys in a landscape developed by people. The historical information on southern settlements and colonies on power-line pylons dates from the time the book was prepared, not from a present-day census. Reports of its disappearance from the western part of the Chüy Valley are likewise retrospective.

The birds build their nests on buildings, old trees and engineering structures. The article describes a clutch of two to five eggs, incubated by both parents. The listed food includes amphibians, reptiles, small fish, large insects and rodents. Autumn departure is given as August–September.

The draining of marshes, changes to feeding areas, pesticides and the destruction of nests are named as threats. The authors propose identifying and protecting nesting sites and carrying out awareness work. Old approximate figures are not used as an estimate of the country’s population. The Russian and English versions disagree on the subspecies; this card keeps only the species rank and makes no claim about subspecies.
According to the account, birds arrive in spring at the beginning of March and depart in August–September. Nests were built on buildings, trees and power-line pylons.
Amphibians, lizards, snakes, small fish, large insects, arachnids and rodents are listed in the 2006 account.
The clutch contains 2–5 eggs; both male and female incubate. According to the book, the chicks leave the nest after 70–72 days.
Historical information relates to the Fergana Valley margins in southern Kyrgyzstan; occasional sightings on passage are known from Issyk-Kul. Present-day occurrence has not been updated.
Historically, lowland and foothill river valleys in a cultivated landscape, including old settlements.

The Eurasian spoonbill is listed in the 2006 national edition as Platalea leucorodia. The historical account reports rare sightings on passage and in winter in the Chüy Valley, the Issyk-Kul basin and on high-mountain lakes. A suggestion of former nesting in the west of Issyk-Kul is not treated as confirmation of present-day breeding. The source gives no systematic data on numbers.

Wetlands and water bodies with muddy shores are important for the spoonbill. It gathers food in the shallows with side-to-side sweeps of its bill; the article lists tadpoles, molluscs, frogs, aquatic insects and plant food. The descriptions of massive nests in trees and a clutch of four eggs relate to the biology of the species, not to proven local nesting.

The main threat noted is the draining of sites suitable for resting and breeding for agriculture. Illegal shooting is also mentioned. The book’s recommendations are to preserve wetlands and shoreline trees. The structured field for local breeding has been left as unknown; the historical national category does not stand in for the global IUCN status.
According to the book, it feeds in shallow water mainly in the morning and evening, sweeping its head and bill from side to side.
The national article lists tadpoles, molluscs, frogs, aquatic insects and, less often, plant food.
Historically rare on passage and in winter in the Chüy Valley, the Issyk-Kul basin and on lakes of the Inner Tien Shan; former nesting is presumed.
Wetlands, mainly lower river reaches and water bodies with muddy shores.

The Himalayan griffon appears in the 2006 book of Kyrgyzstan under the name Gyps himalayensis. The historical information relates to the high-mountain belts of the Tien Shan and Pamir-Alay. Subalpine and alpine habitats where wild ungulates and domestic animals occur are important. The article names rock outcrops as nesting sites.

It is a resident bird that feeds on carrion. The account describes single pairs and breeding colonies, incubation beginning in March and observations of a nest with a single egg. The authors explicitly stress how scant the information on breeding is. Dated route counts and a gathering of birds in the Ak-Jilga area characterise the sites surveyed; they are not an estimate of the whole national population.

Reduced availability of carrion and the eating of poisoned baits laid for wolves are named as threats, along with direct killing. Protection of colonies and the organisation of monitoring without disturbing the birds are recommended. Proposals for supplementary feeding remain recommendations of the source, not an announced present-day programme. Questions of contact with the Eurasian griffon and possible hybridisation are left open for study in the book; these two precisely accepted species are not automatically merged.
A resident bird; according to the historical account it nests in single pairs and in colonies, and gathers at carrion.
Feeds on carrion; according to the national article, the availability of carcasses of wild and domestic animals matters.
The book reports incubation beginning in March and the finding of a single egg in May; local breeding biology is insufficiently studied.
Historically, the ranges of the Tien Shan and the Alay system listed in the national account; no present-day map has been made.
Subalpine and alpine belts with wild ungulates and domestic animals; rock outcrops for nesting.

The Eurasian griffon is included in the 2006 national book as Gyps fulvus. The account assigns it to the low and middle mountains of the northern and southern margins of the Tien Shan. Its habitats are linked to wild ungulates and concentrations of domestic animals; a dissected rocky landscape is important for nesting. In some areas the species occurs alongside the Himalayan griffon.

According to the article the bird is resident and nests in pairs and colonies. Incubation begins in March, and a single egg is laid. Young that could not yet fly were found in early June. Such historical information describes the biology of the birds surveyed but is no substitute for present-day counts. Local observations of a group at Tuya-Muyun and other sightings are not extrapolated to the whole country.

The availability of carrion is named as the main limiting factor. Poisoned baits laid for wolves and direct killing are dangerous. The authors recommend protecting colonies with small reserves and involving local people in monitoring without disturbing the birds. References to contact with another species are not in themselves proof of taxonomic merging. The historical national category Near Threatened is kept together with the year of the edition, and no global IUCN status is assigned.
According to the account, a resident species nesting in pairs and colonies; the availability of carrion limits its presence.
Its dependence on the carrion of wild and domestic animals for food is explicitly noted among the limiting factors in the national article.
According to the book, incubation begins in March and a single egg is laid; young not yet able to fly were observed in early June.
Historically, the northern and southern margins of the Tien Shan; precise present-day range boundaries have not been updated.
Low and middle mountains with wild ungulates and domestic animals; rocky sections of dissected landscape.

The short-toed eagle is listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan under the name Circaetus gallicus. The historical account gives sightings in the Chüy and Talas valleys, the Issyk-Kul area and southern districts, and nesting sites on several ranges. Its main habitats are described as dry foothills, desert mountains and patches of walnut-fruit forest.

According to the source, it arrives in spring in early April and begins nesting in May. The clutch usually consists of one egg. The Russian and English texts differ on the length of incubation, so this period has been neither chosen nor averaged. Reptiles make up its main food. Scattered old sightings do not allow the present size of the national population to be estimated.

Direct killing, the destruction of nests, disturbance and the shrinking of the food supply as land is developed are named as threats. The authors recommend clarifying population size, studying the biology and the state of food resources, and testing whether the birds can be attracted to artificial nest sites. A reference to historical protection at Sary-Chelek is no substitute for a present-day check of the area’s protection regime. The subspecies heptneri is mentioned only as the national description: no separate subspecies card or independent assessment is created for it.
According to the national account, it arrives in early April and begins nesting in May.
Mainly reptiles, according to the national article.
The book gives one egg as the usual clutch; because the versions disagree, no incubation period has been chosen.
Historical information on the valleys and ranges of Kyrgyzstan is kept as retrospective; present-day presence has not been surveyed.
Dry foothills and desert mountains; the account also names walnut-fruit forests at altitudes of 1500–2200 m.

The pallid harrier is included in the 2006 national edition as Circus macrourus. The account lists the Chüy and At-Bashy valleys, the Issyk-Kul basin and high-mountain areas of the Inner Tien Shan. Open plains and low and middle mountain terrain, including farmland, are suitable for it. All these references come from the historical source.

The bird is described as hunting by flying low over open ground and often resting on the ground. Its food includes mouse-like rodents, lizards, frogs, grasshoppers and the chicks of other birds. The Russian version treats local nesting as possible, while the English one states it more definitely. For this reason general information on ground nests and clutches for the species as a whole has not been turned into proof of breeding in Kyrgyzstan.

There are no systematic population counts; observations at ponds near Bishkek in 2005 are not an overall estimate. Disturbance at breeding sites and direct killing are named as threats. The book recommends protecting suitable sites, limiting the presence of people and domestic animals near nests that have been found, and further monitoring. Independent verification of present-day national presence remains necessary.
According to the account, it hunts by flying over open ground and prefers to rest on the ground; local nesting is only presumed in the Russian version.
Mouse-like rodents, lizards, frogs, grasshoppers and the chicks of other bird species are listed in the book.
Historical sightings in the Chüy and At-Bashy valleys, the Issyk-Kul basin and the syrts of the Inner Tien Shan.
Open plains and low and middle mountains, including developed land; less often high mountains.

The Eurasian water shrew is listed in the 2006 book of Kyrgyzstan under the name Neomys fodiens. The national account classes it as a rare species at the edge of its range. Historical finds are listed for the Issyk-Kul basin, Kungey and Teskey Ala-Too, the Chüy and Suusamyr valleys and the Kyrgyz Range. No new observations or coordinates have been added to this information.

Its habitats are described as woodland and scrub near rivers, lakes and marshy places, from the valleys up to the alpine belt. The animal is active all year round, mainly at night. Invertebrates form the basis of its diet. The book places the breeding season in March–July and reports females with several embryos; gestation data from the European part of the range are not carried over to the local population.

Catches made with differing trapping effort characterise particular surveys rather than national numbers. The main threat named is the conversion of suitable habitats into farmland. Conserving wetland areas and floodplain vegetation, clarifying the distribution and carrying out counts are recommended. A present-day population estimate remains unknown, and the historical national category does not stand in for a global classification.
According to the national account, it is active all year and mainly nocturnal.
According to the article, invertebrates form the basis of its diet; no detailed local composition is given.
The book places the local breeding season in March–July; up to seven embryos have been recorded. European gestation periods have not been extrapolated.
Historical finds in the Issyk-Kul basin, on Kungey and Teskey Ala-Too, in the Chüy and Suusamyr valleys and on the Kyrgyz Range.
Woodland and scrub habitats by lakes, rivers and marshy places, from the valleys up to the alpine belt.

The Bokhara horseshoe bat is described in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan as Rhinolophus bocharicus. The saved GBIF check confirms the binomial, species rank and authorship of Kastschenko and Akimov, 1917. Historical national finds come from the foothills of the Alay and Turkestan ranges. The broad range outside the country given in the article is not automatically carried over to the modern taxonomic concept.

Warm, humid caves in arid foothills are used as roosts. According to the account, the bats stay in their roosts by day, emerge in the evening and before dawn, and hunt over fields, river floodplains and canals. Their main food is soft-bodied insects, including flies, moths and beetles. The source places breeding in late May to early June.

Visits to caves by people cause the bats to abandon their roosts; the authors recommend restricting uncontrolled visits and protecting the places where they live. Old information on small aggregations does not represent a present-day estimate of numbers. The 2009 list keeps the spelling Rinolophus bocharicus: this is documented separately, is not presented as a literal match and is not used in place of direct confirmation from the book.
The English summary of the national account gives a body length of 52–60 mm; no detailed diagnostic description is provided.
Nocturnal, spending the day in roosts; according to the 2006 book it emerges in the evening and before dawn.
Mainly soft-bodied insects: flies, owlet moths, beetles and cuckoo wasps, according to the national article.
According to the national account, the breeding period falls in late May to early June; litter size is not established by this source.
Historical national finds in the northern foothills of the Alay and Turkestan ranges. The book’s broad worldwide range is not asserted for the modern concept.
Arid low foothills; roosts in warm, humid caves, with rivers and canals nearby.

The Asian barbastelle appears in the 2006 national book under the name Barbastella leucomelas. The account describes a rare bat that uses underground roosts in arid mountain areas. The information relates to the historical national concept; present-day presence at the sites named requires a separate survey.

Historical localities are associated with the arid foothills of the Turkestan, Alay and Fergana ranges; the Inner Tien Shan is also mentioned. The bats use rock and loess caves, and abandoned adits are noted in particular for wintering. The book describes seasonal movements: foothill caves in winter and higher parts of the mountains in summer.

Small groups in roosts do not allow total numbers to be established. The authors state plainly that diet and breeding under Kyrgyz conditions have not been studied; this information is left as unknown. Limiting factors have not been established either, so the presence of mites and fleas has not been turned into a proven threat. Protection of habitats and roosts is recommended. The range outside the country in the historical account is not carried over to the modern understanding of the species without a separate check; no new geographical points have been created.
According to the account, it makes seasonal altitudinal movements: it leaves its wintering sites in March–April and moves up into the mountains in summer.
Historical finds in southern Kyrgyzstan in the foothills of the Turkestan, Alay and Fergana ranges, and also in the Inner Tien Shan.
Rock and loess caves in arid foothills; winter roosts also include abandoned adits.

The European free-tailed bat is included in the 2006 book of Kyrgyzstan as Tadarida teniotis. The account describes an inhabitant of rocky areas in the low and middle mountains that uses rock crevices and cave ceilings. The results of a 1992 expedition broadened understanding of its distribution in the country compared with earlier reports, which came only from the surroundings of Osh. However, the number of sites surveyed and bats caught is not a national population estimate.

The species is characterised as migratory, especially in the northern part of its range; its seasonal biology is insufficiently studied. The English summary explicitly mentions a diet of night-flying insects. The Russian and English versions differ on the number of young. For this reason no exact litter size has been chosen, and local breeding is noted as insufficiently studied.

Frequent visits to caves by people are named as a threat; the effect of agricultural chemicals is given as a supposition. The book recommends protecting caves and suitable habitats and carrying out awareness work with local residents. Historical information on protection since 1975 is no substitute for checking current legislation. Data on present-day numbers, movements and the condition of roosts remain unknown.
The book notes migratory behaviour and colonial use of roosts; its seasonal biology is insufficiently studied.
The English summary of the national account explicitly mentions hunting of night-flying insects.
Historical data from the 1992 expedition relate to many surveyed sites in Kyrgyzstan; widespread present-day presence is not claimed.
Rocky areas in the low and middle mountains; roosts in rock crevices and on cave ceilings.

The brown bear is listed in the 2006 national book as Ursus arctos. The account primarily describes the local populations, which the authors assign to the subspecies isabellinus. The historical national assessment does not automatically extend to all the brown bears of the world. The card keeps the species rank and the identity accepted in the register, without creating an additional subspecies record.

In Kyrgyzstan the source associates the bear mainly with mountain areas and lists a number of ranges. The animals usually come out to feed in the morning and evening and may move temporarily in search of food. Winter hibernation and dens in rock clefts are described. The female gives birth to cubs in the den; the specific months of birth are not consistent between the Russian and English versions and are not chosen here. The article used does not set out the composition of the diet.

Old local densities and counts relate to past decades, not to present-day numbers. Poaching and the shrinking of suitable territory are among the threats named. The authors propose creating protected areas where bears concentrate, stepping up action against poaching and studying the local populations. The report of earlier hunting bans remains historical, with no claim about the current legal regime.
According to the book, feeding activity is mostly in the morning and evening; winter hibernation and temporary movements in search of food or when pursued are described.
In the historical account the female usually gives birth to two, less often three, cubs in the den; because the versions disagree, no exact months of birth have been chosen.
Historical information on the mountain areas of Kyrgyzstan relates to the national populations of isabellinus; no map of present-day presence has been made.
According to the national account, mainly mountain areas; winter dens are often in rock clefts.

The beech marten, or stone marten, is described in the 2006 book of Kyrgyzstan under the name Martes foina. The historical account reports its presence on the country’s mountain ranges and links the local populations with the subspecies intermedia. The accepted species rank of the card is not in itself confirmation of the subspecies diagnosis.

Its favoured habitats are rocky piles and screes in the middle and high mountains. It is a predator that does not hibernate, active mainly at dusk and at night; by day it uses shelters. Mouse-like rodents, pikas and birds are named as its food. The article describes individual home ranges and the possibility of moving between them. Breeding involves a summer rut and the appearance of young the following spring.

An old local density figure has not been turned into a present-day national estimate. The authors discuss possible limiting factors tentatively: food supply, poaching, fecundity and snowy winters. The English summary recommends reducing grazing in suitable habitats and combating poaching; these proposals are not treated as a programme already carried out. Detailed appearance, present-day counts and current legal status require separate confirmation. The national category is kept together with the year of the historical edition.
According to the account, it is active all year, mainly at dusk and at night; by day it stays in shelters, and it uses individual home ranges.
Mouse-like rodents and pikas; also birds, according to the national article.
According to the book, the rut is in June–August and the young are born the following spring, in April–May; a litter contains 2–5 young.
The historical account gives the mountain ranges of Kyrgyzstan; present-day numbers and distribution have not been surveyed.
Rocky piles of large boulders and screes in the middle and high mountains.

The Central Asian otter is listed in the 2006 national book under the species Lutra lutra, with the local subspecies seistanica indicated. The historical national category relates to this local concept and does not mean that all populations of the species worldwide are critically threatened. The card keeps the accepted species rank, and the subspecies is not added as a second taxon.

The account describes former occurrence in waters of several river basins of Kyrgyzstan. For the time the book was prepared, presence in the Alay Valley is named; survival in other basins was presumed. These reports are not used as confirmed presence today. Its habitats are associated with the banks of rivers and lakes with floodplain trees and shrubs or rock debris.

The article describes its biology under the country’s conditions as unstudied. Detailed appearance, a direct description of diet and breeding have therefore been left unknown. The Russian version gives no numbers, and a brief English suggestion of a few pairs has not been taken as an estimate. Killing and the depletion of fish stocks are named as threats. The authors recommend surveying the presumed habitats and creating a protected area in the Alay Valley. These recommendations and the historical hunting ban are no substitute for checking the present state of protection.
Historically, the basins of Issyk-Kul, the Chatkal and the Naryn, and the Alay Valley. The book’s references to possible survival in other basins have not been taken as confirmed present-day records.
Banks of rivers and lakes with floodplain trees and shrubs or rock debris; the account notes the availability of fish in the waters.

The small five-toed jerboa is described in the 2006 national book under the name Allactaga elater. The historical national information relates primarily to the Chüy and Talas valleys. The species is associated with relatively flat desert areas with sparse grasses and shrubs; it avoids steep slopes and developed irrigated land. This information is not a new map of present-day presence.

The animals use permanent and temporary burrows and come out at night. In the book, the timing of winter hibernation and spring emergence differs between the warmer Chüy Valley and the Talas Valley. Breeding also begins at different times; no single date is assigned for the whole country. The food listed includes green parts of plants, seeds, bulbs, tubers and rhizomes, as well as insects.

Night-time route sightings reflect a particular counting method and have not been extrapolated to national numbers. The main threat is the transformation of habitats through ploughing and irrigation of land. The authors recommend conserving characteristic habitats. The subspecies vinogradovi is mentioned in the article but does not receive a card of its own. The historical category Lower Risk relates to the national edition, and this publication does not assert the present-day status or the date of the author citation.
According to the book, it is nocturnal and lives in burrows; winter hibernation and spring emergence occur at different times in the Chüy and Talas valleys.
Green parts of plants, seeds, bulbs, tubers and rhizomes of ephemerals and ephemeroids; also insects, according to the national account.
The book gives the start of breeding as March in the Chüy Valley and later in the Talas Valley; 2–5 embryos have been recorded, and some individuals have two litters.
Historically, the Chüy and Talas valleys; precise present-day distribution limits have not been surveyed.
Relatively flat arid areas with sparse herbaceous and shrub vegetation; steep slopes and irrigated land are avoided.

The tapered net-cap is included in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan under the spelling Dictyocephalus attenuatus. The 2009 list uses Dictyocephalos attenuatus; it is this form that Species Fungorum and an exact GBIF match confirm. The link was established from the epithet and the authors of the name, not from the outward resemblance of the fungus. The old article’s statement that it is the only species in its genus is not reproduced here as a present-day taxonomic fact.

The fruiting body is described as tall, with a broadened net-like head and a deeply furrowed stem that hardens as it matures. A cup-shaped remnant of the outer covering remains at the base. Young fruiting bodies are paler than mature ones; a characteristic smell is noted directly in the national account. Its habitats are associated with the clay and sandy deserts of the valleys and foothills of northern Kyrgyzstan.

The source openly acknowledges a lack of biological information and the absence of data on limiting factors. For this reason the mode of nutrition, a detailed life cycle and threats have not been supplemented with guesses. The 2006 recommendations include conserving habitats and educating the public. Present-day numbers and the current state of the national records require a separate check.

According to the 2006 account, the fruiting body is up to 27 cm tall, with a net-like head and a furrowed stem that later becomes woody; there is a cup-shaped volva at the base. The colour changes from whitish yellow to yellowish brown.
A terrestrial fungus of arid habitats; the national account marks the details of its biology as unstudied.
The 2006 book gives northern Kyrgyzstan. Present-day presence and coordinates have not been confirmed.
Clay and sandy deserts of valleys and foothills; the national account notes outcrops of Jurassic deposits.

Tschitscherin’s root borer is given in the 2006 national account as Prionus (Pogonartron) tschitscherini. The name accepted for the card, Pogonarthron tschitscherini, is confirmed by an exact taxonomic match and by the 2017 work of Danilevsky and Shapovalov, which lists the earlier combinations. The difference in the year of authorship between GBIF and the scientific paper has been left for bibliographic proofreading; no date is asserted in the scientific name on the card.

According to the national description, it is a stocky brown beetle with a convex body, well-developed eyes and, in the male, long comb-like antennae. Its historical range is associated with the foothills and low mountains around the Fergana Valley. The species lives in pistachio open woodland and the steppe belt, in areas where the soil and vegetation cover has been preserved. The larvae feed on the roots of perennial wormwoods; the males fly at dusk.

The article considers the life cycle insufficiently studied. Suppositions about the length of development and flightless females have not been turned into established facts. Agricultural development, excessive grazing and pesticides are among the threats named. Conserving habitats, reducing pressure on them and studying the biology are recommended. Old observations do not provide a present-day estimate of numbers.

The account describes a beetle 15.5–18.5 mm long with a stocky, convex body, mainly brown colouring, large eyes and, in the male, long comb-like antennae. Females were not known to the authors of the 2006 article.
In the national account the males hide by day in shelters on the ground and fly from dusk; flight is recorded from late May to the last third of August.
According to the national account, the larvae feed on the roots of perennial wormwoods.
The national account links the records with the foothills around the Fergana Valley, including the Chatkal, Fergana and Kichik-Alay ranges; this is historical information.
Pistachio open woodland and steppe areas in the foothills and low mountains with undisturbed soil and vegetation, rocky outliers and rock outcrops; historically 600–1100 m.

Knorring’s haw-tree appears in the 2006 book and the 2009 list under the name Crataegus knorringiana. The accepted species name is confirmed by an exact GBIF match. The national account describes the species as a narrow endemic and notes individual plants in several mountain districts of Kyrgyzstan. This information is kept as a historical description, without new coordinates or numerical estimates.

It is a small tree with narrowly elliptic or ovate, slightly lobed leaves. The small yellow fruits contain five distinctly pitted stones. Its habitats are associated with tree and shrub vegetation in river valleys and with stony and fine-soil slopes of the lower and middle mountain belts. It flowers in late April and early May and the fruits ripen in September; reproduction is described as by seed.

The main threats noted are economic development of sites, use of the trees for fuel and poor regeneration. The authors recommend protecting the remaining plants from felling and young plants from damage by livestock. The Russian and English versions differ on whether there are data on cultivation; successful cultivation is not claimed. Present-day numbers, the condition of young plants and whether the old recommendations have actually been implemented all require survey.
According to the account, a tree up to 5–6 m tall with narrowly elliptic or ovate, slightly lobed leaves. The fruits are small and yellow, with five strongly pitted stones.
The book notes solitary plants and very poor regeneration.
According to the book, it flowers in late April to early May and the fruits ripen in September; reproduction is by seed and regeneration is poor.
Historically recorded from the Chichkan Valley and the Chatkal, Fergana and Alay Ranges; current observations are not confirmed.
Tree and shrub communities of river valleys; stony and fine-soil slopes of the lower and middle mountain belts.

The dwarf ammopiptanth is included in the 2006 national book and the 2009 list as Ammopiptanthus nanus. Its accepted name is confirmed by an exact GBIF match. The historical local records relate to the Kokomeren basin and the Kavak-Too and Jumgal-Too mountains. A count for 1979 mentioned in the article is not used as a present-day estimate of numbers.

It is an evergreen shrub with twisting branches, silvery-hairy leaves and yellow flowers in dense racemes. The fruits are oblong pods. The national account associates it with slopes of variegated sedimentary strata. Flowering is described in June–July and fruiting in July–August; it can reproduce both from seed and vegetatively. Historical trials in a botanical garden were unsuccessful: young plants coped poorly with the following winter.

The book names collection of plants, economic activity and washing out by mudflows. The present-day impact of each factor has not been assessed separately. The Russian version recommends a reserve on the Minkush, while the English version already speaks of protection there; the actual regime has not been chosen by assumption. This entry keeps the recommendations to protect habitats and leaves present-day numbers and legal status unknown.
According to the book, an evergreen shrub up to 1.5 m tall with twisting branches, silvery-hairy broadly elliptic leaves, yellow flowers in dense racemes and oblong pods.
According to the national account, it flowers in June–July and fruits in July–August; it reproduces from seed and vegetatively.
The historical national account gives Kavak-Too and Jumgal-Too in the Kokomeren basin; no present-day observations have been created.
Slopes of variegated sedimentary strata in the historically recorded mountain districts of the Kokomeren basin.

The short-winged bladder-senna is named in the 2006 national book and the 2009 list as Colutea brachyptera. The same accepted name is confirmed by an exact GBIF taxonomic match. The historical account assigns the plant to the Fergana and Alay Ranges, without a present-day assessment of surviving sites or population sizes.

It is a low deciduous shrub. The grey older branches differ from the white-barked first-year shoots; the leaves consist of several pairs of rounded leaflets. The yellow flowers are borne in drooping racemes, and the ripe fruits are large membranous pods. Its habitats are associated with weathering products of red sandstones and conglomerates, stony slopes and rocky gorges in the foothills and the lower mountain belt.

The book gives flowering in May–June and fruiting in June–July; reproduction is mainly by seed, with vegetative reproduction noted as rare.
