There are no quantitative data on numbers and no information on cultivation. The threats named are economic works and mass collection of flowering plants. Population counts and botanical reserves at sites of concentration are recommended. Its earlier inclusion in protection lists is not presented as an independent check of the regime currently in force.
A deciduous shrub up to 1 m tall with paired rounded leaflets, yellow flowers in drooping racemes and elliptic membranous pods up to 5 cm long.
According to the book, it flowers in May–June and fruits in June–July; it reproduces from seed and only very rarely vegetatively.
The historical range covers the Fergana and Alay Ranges in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan; there are no new localities.
Weathering products of red sandstones and conglomerates; stony, rubbly and rocky gorge slopes in the foothills and the lower mountain belt.

Eugenia’s primrose is included in the 2006 national edition and the 2009 list as Primula eugeniae. The accepted species name has an exact GBIF confirmation. The account calls the plant a rare narrow endemic of the western part of the Fergana Range, known from the Baubash-Ata mountains. This is a historical national reference, with no claim that it is present at every site today.

It is a perennial rhizomatous plant with broad toothed leaves on long petioles. The pale yellow flowers form an umbel-like inflorescence. Its habitats are rock crevices in the alpine and nival belts. The numerical flower sizes in the printed article look doubtful in their units and have not been carried over to this entry. They must not be quietly corrected by replacing centimetres with millimetres.

The book gives reproduction by seed and fruiting in August, and acknowledges that regeneration in the wild has not been studied. A tentative flowering month from the English text is likewise not accepted as established. Intensive economic activity is named as the limiting factor. The authors propose a botanical reserve and bringing this ornamental plant into cultivation. Present-day numbers, the success of cultivation and the implementation of these measures remain unknown.

A perennial rhizomatous plant with broadly elliptic toothed leaves on long petioles and pale yellow flowers in an umbel-like inflorescence. Doubtful flower sizes from the printed description are omitted.
According to the national account, it reproduces from seed and fruits in August; natural regeneration has not been studied and the flowering period has not been established.
The historical account gives the western part of the Fergana Range, the Baubash-Ata mountains; there are no new observations.
Rock crevices in the alpine and nival belts.

The Alai physochlaina is included in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan under the name Physochlaina alaica; the same name appears in the 2009 list and is confirmed by an exact GBIF match. The national account treats the plant as a rare, narrowly local species of the Alay and Turkestan Ranges. The historical information has not been turned into new geographical observations.

This perennial produces several erect hairy stems with broadly ovate leaves. The dirty-cream flowers are marked with dark spots; in fruit the calyx becomes leathery. The species is described from the shade of rocks, beneath shrubs and in open glades in juniper communities. Reproduction is by seed; it flowers in May–June and the fruits ripen at the end of July.

The national article links damage to the plants with unregulated grazing and pasture improvement works. The authors recommend protected botanical sites where it grows. No quantitative estimate of numbers is given. The Russian version contains no information on cultivation, while the English one mentions an unsuccessful attempt to bring it into cultivation; no definite outcome has been chosen. Toxicity, medicinal use and other properties not described in the checked account are not inferred from its membership of the family.
According to the book, a perennial with erect hairy and glandular stems up to 50 cm, broadly ovate leaves and dirty-cream flowers with dark spots; the calyx is leathery in fruit.
The national account gives reproduction by seed, flowering in May–June and ripening of the fruits at the end of July.
Historically recorded from the Turkestan and Alay Ranges and the Isfara, Sokh and Shakhimardan valleys in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
Shade of rocks, sites beneath shrubs and open glades in juniper communities.

Olga’s Chinese trumpet-creeper is listed in the 2006 national book and the 2009 list as Incarvillea olgae. This accepted name is confirmed by an exact GBIF match. The historical account links its localities in Kyrgyzstan with the northern slope of the Alay Range, between the Shakhimardan and Sokh rivers. Neither new observations nor confirmation of the current state of individual populations have been added.

It is a perennial plant with dissected leaves and a loose terminal inflorescence. The large flowers are mostly pinkish-purple, less often white; the fruit is an elongated many-seeded capsule. The book gives pebbly river floodplains and stony or clayey slopes. Flowering is recorded in June–July and reproduction is by seed. The difference between the language versions on when fruiting ends has not been resolved by assumption.

Threats are linked to collection of the ornamental flowers and geological works. The authors report earlier successful cultivation in a botanical garden and intolerance of shading. An inventory of populations, additional botanical reserves and the resumption of cultivation are recommended. The photograph shows a cultivated plant in Poland and serves as an illustration of the species; it does not prove its presence or numbers in Kyrgyzstan.

According to the book, a perennial up to 1 m tall with pinnately dissected leaves, a loose terminal inflorescence and large pinkish-purple, less often white flowers; the fruit is an elongated many-seeded capsule.
According to the national account, the plant does not tolerate shading; earlier trials of cultivation in a botanical garden are described as successful.
According to the book, it reproduces from seed and flowers in June–July. The exact fruiting period has not been chosen from the diverging RU/EN wording.
Historically recorded in Kyrgyzstan between the Shakhimardan and Sokh rivers on the northern slope of the Alay Range; there are no new localities.
Pebbly river floodplains and alluvial fans of stony and clayey slopes; the old account gives a range of 700–2500 m.

The wrapped alpine saw-wort is included in the 2006 national book and the 2009 list as Saussurea involucrata. The accepted name is confirmed by an exact GBIF taxonomic match. The account treats the plant as a rare species at the edge of its range in Kyrgyzstan; the old qualitative description has not been turned into a current quantitative estimate.

It is a high-mountain perennial with a short or well-developed simple stem. Several flower heads with tubular violet flowers are gathered into a dense inflorescence and surrounded by large pale bract leaves. The national article associates its habitats with rocky slopes, boulder screes and moraines of the alpine and nival belts. In Kyrgyzstan, areas of the Northern and Central Tien Shan are recorded historically; the present-day distribution has not been checked separately.

The book gives flowering in June–July and fruiting in August, with reproduction by seed. There are no data on cultivation. Intensive summer grazing and unorganised tourism are named as limiting factors; the English text specifies collection of the flowers. The authors recommend conserving habitats and setting up botanical reserves. Food, medicinal and other properties not confirmed by the checked account are not included in this entry.

According to the book, a perennial 15–35 cm tall with a short or simple stem, hairy leaves and tubular violet flowers. The flower heads are gathered into a dense inflorescence surrounded by large pale bract leaves.
According to the national account, it flowers in June–July and fruits in August; it reproduces from seed.
The historical account gives the Küngöy and Teskey Ala-Too, Ak-Shyirak and the upper parts of the Sary-Jaz, Inylchek and Kuilyu basins. There are no new observations.
Rocky slopes, stony screes and moraines of the alpine and nival belts.

A perennial campion of rocks and stony slopes, included in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account contains the following information. The national account describes it as a rare species with a restricted distribution. There was no information on cultivation, and no special studies of the causes of its rarity are cited. The 2006 Russian account gives reproduction by seed, flowering in June–July and fruiting in July–August. The English summary on the same page reports a lack of biological data; the information here follows the Russian account. The book’s historical records relate to the southern slope of the Suusamyr Range, Kavak-Too, Moldo-Too and Kokiyrim. The present-day state of these localities is not confirmed. Recommendation of the 2006 edition: to create a botanical reserve on the southern slope of the Suusamyr Range to protect a complex of rare plants.

A herbaceous perennial with a dense caudex and erect stems up to 40 cm tall. The narrow basal leaves are hairless; the drooping flowers are gathered in a raceme. The greenish petals are deeply divided into narrow lobes.
The national account describes it as a rare species with a restricted distribution. There was no information on cultivation, and no special studies of the causes of its rarity are cited.

The 2006 Russian account gives reproduction by seed, flowering in June–July and fruiting in July–August. The English summary on the same page reports a lack of biological data; the information here follows the Russian account.
The book’s historical records relate to the southern slope of the Suusamyr Range, Kavak-Too, Moldo-Too and Kokiyrim. The present-day state of these localities is not confirmed.
Rock crevices and stony mountain slopes.

A perennial plant of clayey limestone slopes in the Alay Valley, from the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account contains the following information. The national edition characterises the plant as an extremely rare local endemic. It is associated with open slopes with sparse plant cover; the account contains no information on cultivation. According to the 2006 book, it reproduces from seed, flowers in June and fruits in July. The Russian account gives the Alay Valley, Kyzyl-Eshme and the Kashka-Suu basin. This is historical information, not confirmation of present-day finds. According to the 2006 edition, unregulated grazing and excessive grazing pressure hinder the regeneration of the plants. The 2006 book proposes creating a botanical reserve in the Kashka-Suu basin, at sites where populations are concentrated.
A plant greyish with dense fine hairs, with a branched caudex that becomes woody. The leaves form a basal rosette; the violet petals reach 20–25 mm. The fruits are flattened, broadly linear siliques.
The national edition characterises the plant as an extremely rare local endemic. It is associated with open slopes with sparse plant cover; the account contains no information on cultivation.
According to the 2006 book, it reproduces from seed, flowers in June and fruits in July.
The Russian account gives the Alay Valley, Kyzyl-Eshme and the Kashka-Suu basin. This is historical information, not confirmation of present-day finds.
Clayey and limestone deposits of the middle and upper mountain belts.

A shrub of stony low mountains, described in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan under the name Spiraeanthus schrenkianus. The 2006 national account contains the following information. According to the historical description, the growing season begins in April. Natural regeneration is poor. The book reports an unsuccessful attempt to grow it in the Bishkek botanical garden in 1955–1958 because of competition from other shrubs. It flowers in June for about 15–20 days; the fruits ripen from the end of July to September. The account describes seed germination but notes the absence of seedlings and young plants in natural conditions. The historical national account confirms its inclusion for Kyrgyzstan. The Russian part names the Mailuu-Suu basin, the English part the surroundings of Maimak. These conflicting references have not been merged into a confirmed range; the present-day locality needs to be checked. The 2006 book gives unregulated grazing and cutting of shrubs for fuel. Recommendations of 2006: to clarify the state of the populations, set up a botanical reserve and repeat cultivation trials with a view to possible reintroduction.

A shrub up to 3 m tall with a dense crown, greyish-yellow cracking bark and small leaflets in paripinnate leaves. Fragrant white-and-pink flowers form panicles at the tips of the current year’s shoots.

According to the historical description, the growing season begins in April. Natural regeneration is poor. The book reports an unsuccessful attempt to grow it in the Bishkek botanical garden in 1955–1958 because of competition from other shrubs.

It flowers in June for about 15–20 days; the fruits ripen from the end of July to September. The account describes seed germination but notes the absence of seedlings and young plants in natural conditions.

The historical national account confirms its inclusion for Kyrgyzstan. The Russian part names the Mailuu-Suu basin, the English part the surroundings of Maimak. These conflicting references have not been merged into a confirmed range; the present-day locality needs to be checked.
Stony slopes of low mountains; according to the national account, the plants form small groups.

A hairy perennial of the stony foothill plains of the western Issyk-Kul area, from the 2006 Red Data Book. The 2006 national account contains the following information. The historical account links the plant’s rarity with human pressure and poor regeneration during drought. The edition used contains no data on successful cultivation. According to the 2006 edition, reproduction is by seed; it flowers in July and fruits in August. The historical area of finds in the book is the western part of the Issyk-Kul basin. The present-day limits of its distribution have not been established by this study. Spring grazing and other human impacts are given in the account as limiting factors. Drought is unfavourable for regeneration from seed; present-day losses have not been quantified. The 2006 book recommends population counts and bringing the plant into cultivation at the Botanical Garden of the National Academy of Sciences of the Kyrgyz Republic.
A perennial herb with dense shaggy hairs, a stout taproot and creeping stems. The leaves are imparipinnate, each flowering stalk bears a single red flower, and the pods are oblong.
The historical account links the plant’s rarity with human pressure and poor regeneration during drought. The edition used contains no data on successful cultivation.
According to the 2006 edition, reproduction is by seed; it flowers in July and fruits in August.
The historical area of finds in the book is the western part of the Issyk-Kul basin. The present-day limits of its distribution have not been established by this study.
Stony foothill plains with desert and semi-desert vegetation.

A perennial sweetvetch of walnut-fruit forests and tall-herb meadows, from the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account contains the following information. A relict plant of forest communities, described in the national edition as rare, occurring singly or in small groups. Historical information on its rarity is not a present-day numerical estimate. According to the 2006 book, it reproduces from seed, flowers in June and fruits in July–August. Historically recorded from the Chatkal, Uzun-Akhmat, Fergana and Alay Ranges, including Sary-Chelek, Kara-Shoro and Arslanbob. No new finds are claimed here. The 2006 account links its decline with human impact on the forests and haymaking. Historical recommendations: to clarify the range and numbers, to create botanical reserves at sites where populations are concentrated, and to study bringing it into cultivation.

A herbaceous perennial up to 60 cm tall, with hairless stems and pinnate leaves. The pinkish-lilac flowers are gathered in dense racemes; the jointed pods are usually covered with short fine bristles, which are absent on some plants.
A relict plant of forest communities, described in the national edition as rare, occurring singly or in small groups. Historical information on its rarity is not a present-day numerical estimate.
According to the 2006 book, it reproduces from seed, flowers in June and fruits in July–August.
Historically recorded from the Chatkal, Uzun-Akhmat, Fergana and Alay Ranges, including Sary-Chelek, Kara-Shoro and Arslanbob. No new finds are claimed here.
Walnut and other broadleaved forests, shrub thickets and tall-herb meadows; the book notes that it extends into the subalpine belt.

A small rock-dwelling subshrub of the Naryn canyon, listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account provides the following information. The book describes the plant as a narrowly distributed rock species confined to a small stretch of the canyon. Reports of very low numbers come from the historical account; no data on cultivation are given. The national account records reproduction by seed and flowering until September; the English summary gives the period more precisely as July–September. The historical locality is the Naryn valley in the foothill part of the Fergana Valley; the English summary names the stretch between Kara-Kul and the mouth of the Kara-Suu. No present-day survey has been carried out. The 2006 edition lists economic works that disturb the habitats and the picking of flowering plants, which reduces regeneration. Historical recommendations: establish the state of the populations and set aside protected sites where the plants are concentrated.

A subshrub with numerous slender stems 4–12 cm tall. The small, dense, broadly ovate leaves and the stems look glaucous because of their thick hairs. Short, dense inflorescences are borne at the stem tips and in the axils of the upper leaves.

The book describes the plant as a narrowly distributed rock species confined to a small stretch of the canyon. Reports of very low numbers come from the historical account; no data on cultivation are given.
The national account records reproduction by seed and flowering until September; the English summary gives the period more precisely as July–September.

The historical locality is the Naryn valley in the foothill part of the Fergana Valley; the English summary names the stretch between Kara-Kul and the mouth of the Kara-Suu. No present-day survey has been carried out.
Rocks and rock crevices of the lower mountain belt in the Naryn canyon.

A hairy perennial of the stony slopes of the Alay Range, listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account provides the following information. The national edition classes the plant as a rare local endemic. Grazing pressure and the picking of flowering shoots are reported for its habitats; the book has no information on growing it in cultivation. Reproduces by seed. The Russian account combines flowering and fruiting in the period May–August; the English summary gives a wider range of dates. The exact present-day phenology has not been established. The historical record in the national account is the Shakhimardan basin in the Alay Range. No new coordinates or records have been added. The historical account cites the picking of flowers and excessive grazing pressure. In 2006 the recommendations were a ban on picking flowers, sustainable use of pastures and the creation of a botanical reserve where the populations are concentrated.

A perennial herb with a slender branching rhizome and weak ascending stems 5–15 cm tall. The small, roundish-ovate leaves are densely covered with long hairs. The corolla is red and yellow, with a yellow patch and dark dots on the lower lip.

The national edition classes the plant as a rare local endemic. Grazing pressure and the picking of flowering shoots are reported for its habitats; the book has no information on growing it in cultivation.

Reproduces by seed. The Russian account combines flowering and fruiting in the period May–August; the English summary gives a wider range of dates. The exact present-day phenology has not been established.
The historical record in the national account is the Shakhimardan basin in the Alay Range. No new coordinates or records have been added.
Stony and gravelly slopes and screes of the middle mountain belt.

A subshrub of the stony low mountains of the Western Tien Shan, listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account provides the following information. According to the national account, the plant is known from a small number of sites in the Western Tien Shan. The edition mentions cultivation at the Tashkent Botanical Garden; this is historical experience, not confirmation that it is in cultivation in Kyrgyzstan today. According to the 2006 book, it reproduces by seed, flowers in June–July and fruits in July–August. In Kyrgyzstan the Chatkal basin is given historically; outside the country, parts of the mountain systems of Uzbekistan are named. No present-day records are claimed in this package. The account notes the small size of the populations and damage to some of the stands from road building. Recommendation of the 2006 edition: establish botanical reserves where the populations are concentrated.

A subshrub with a long rhizome and a well-developed caudex. The oblong leaves are green above and white-felted beneath. The yellow two-lipped flowers are arranged in closely spaced false whorls; the fruit consists of nutlets.

According to the national account, the plant is known from a small number of sites in the Western Tien Shan. The edition mentions cultivation at the Tashkent Botanical Garden; this is historical experience, not confirmation that it is in cultivation in Kyrgyzstan today.
According to the 2006 book, it reproduces by seed, flowers in June–July and fruits in July–August.
In Kyrgyzstan the Chatkal basin is given historically; outside the country, parts of the mountain systems of Uzbekistan are named. No present-day records are claimed in this package.
Stony and fine-gravelly slopes of the lower mountain belt.

A stemless perennial of the stony slopes of the Alay, listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account provides the following information. The national book treats the plant as a rare local endemic with very small populations. There is no information on cultivation; the plant's ornamental appeal does not make it acceptable to collect wild plants. According to the historical account, flowering and fruiting take place in June–July, and reproduction is by seed. The book gives the basins of the Shakhimardan and the Isfayram-Say and the surroundings of Kurban-Kul in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. The present state of the localities has not been checked. The 2006 account names economic activity and disturbance of the limited habitats as threats. Historical recommendations: study the state of the populations, establish a botanical reserve where the plants are concentrated and investigate bringing the species into cultivation.

A low, stemless plant with a thick vertical root and a basal rosette of oblong-ovate leaves. Pinkish-violet, long-tubed flowers develop at the base of the rosette on short pedicels. The fruit is a two-celled capsule.

The national book treats the plant as a rare local endemic with very small populations. There is no information on cultivation; the plant's ornamental appeal does not make it acceptable to collect wild plants.
According to the historical account, flowering and fruiting take place in June–July, and reproduction is by seed.
The book gives the basins of the Shakhimardan and the Isfayram-Say and the surroundings of Kurban-Kul in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. The present state of the localities has not been checked.
Stony mountain slopes and rocks; the English summary places the habitats in the middle mountain belt.

A low shrub of stony slopes with lobed leaves, listed in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The 2006 national account provides the following information. The national book describes the shrub as a relict with a fragmented range and poor regeneration from seed. The counts from past decades given in it have not been carried over into the present-day population field. The book records reproduction by seed, with natural regeneration almost absent. The flowering dates disagree: the Russian text gives July–August, the English one May. No single confirmed period is established here. In Kyrgyzstan the historical account names the Kök-Suu Gorge above Kurban-Köl in the Alay Range; the parts of the range outside the country lie in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Present-day records have not been confirmed. According to the 2006 account, the dangers are the development of habitats, cutting for fuel and the lack of regeneration from seed. Historical recommendations: study the biology, ecology and state of the populations, and establish a reserve in the Kurban-Köl basin.
A squat shrub up to 1.5 m tall with old, peeling grey bark. The leaves are small, some of them noticeably lobed or cut. The axillary flowers are paired; the berries are red and globular.

The national book describes the shrub as a relict with a fragmented range and poor regeneration from seed. The counts from past decades given in it have not been carried over into the present-day population field.

The book records reproduction by seed, with natural regeneration almost absent. The flowering dates disagree: the Russian text gives July–August, the English one May. No single confirmed period is established here.

In Kyrgyzstan the historical account names the Kök-Suu Gorge above Kurban-Köl in the Alay Range; the parts of the range outside the country lie in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Present-day records have not been confirmed.
Coarse boulder aprons beneath limestone cliffs, and stony and gravelly slopes among shrubs, meadow-steppe vegetation and open juniper woodland at altitudes of 2000–3000 m.

A perennial bellflower of crevices in marble cliffs of the Western Tien Shan, listed in the 2006 Red Data Book. The 2006 national account provides the following information. The book classes the plant among the rare endemics of the Western Tien Shan with a restricted distribution. When the edition was prepared, there was no information on cultivation and no special protection measures. According to the 2006 account, reproduction is by seed; flowering is in May–August and fruiting in June–September. The historical national account gives the Talas and Fergana Ranges. According to the book, flowering takes place in July–August and the fruit ripens in August–September. The small size of the populations is described qualitatively. These words do not allow the number of plants in the country to be established, and the prepared package contains no recent comparable counts. Grazing pressure and the picking of flowers are named as limiting factors.

In 2006 the recommendations were to conserve habitats, monitor populations and ban the picking of flowers. This record does not claim that these measures have already been implemented. The historical national VU category is kept separate from a present-day global assessment, which is not assigned here. An illustration from the Flora of Tajikistan is labelled as a foreign example of the species and is not used as evidence of its present-day occurrence in Kyrgyzstan.

A perennial about 3–15 cm tall. The leaves are densely white-felted; the basal leaves are long-stalked and twice or almost three times pinnately dissected. The flower heads are solitary, on long felted stalks; the ray florets are white.
The historical account describes the populations as small; their present-day dynamics and exact sizes have not been established.
According to the 2006 book, it flowers in July–August and fruits in August–September. Details of pollination and regeneration have not been confirmed.

The historical list includes the Küngöy and Teskey Ala-Too, the Fergana and Kyrgyz Ranges, and the Sary-Jaz and Kaindy basins. The overall range given in the book also includes other mountains of Central Asia; present-day local finds are not established.
Mountain river shingle, moraines, stony slopes and screes of the upper mountain belt.

The greater flamingo is a waterbird historically included in the Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan as a rare vagrant. The heading of the 2006 account uses the broad old name Phoenicopterus ruber, but the text itself explicitly specifies the local form P. ruber roseus Pallas, 1811. It is this form that corresponds to the accepted Phoenicopterus roseus and to the line in the national list. The present-day American P. ruber does not replace this concept.

The book gives single records and small groups on Issyk-Kul, including a museum specimen from 1933 and winter observations from the late 1990s and early 2000s. The Russian text and the English summary differ in some geographical wording; this record does not refine them with present-day coordinates. This evidence shows historical vagrant occurrences, not a stable breeding population in the country.

The biology of colonial nesting on shallow salt lakes described in the book refers to the species as a whole. Neither the presence of a colony nor its size in Kyrgyzstan follows from this information. The recommendations on protecting passage and wintering sites are likewise historical in nature.

The national NT category is tied to the 2006 edition. Present-day numbers in Kyrgyzstan are not confirmed, and the numerical sizes of old groups have not been transferred to the national population field. The record requires scientific review and does not claim present-day nesting.

General description of the species from the Illustrated Red Data Book of Birds of South Africa (2015): the plumage is pale pink, the upper wing coverts are bright red and the flight feathers black; young birds are greyer. These features do not constitute confirmation of an observation in Kyrgyzstan.
According to the national account, a rare vagrant. Changes in lake levels and salinity affect where colonies are located across the overall range; no colonies have been established in Kyrgyzstan.
According to the book's general description of the species, it feeds on small crustaceans, molluscs, larvae and the seeds of aquatic plants, filtering water and mud with its bill.
The book describes colonial nests on shallow salt lakes, with both parents taking part in incubation. This information applies to the species in general and does not prove breeding in Kyrgyzstan.
The historical records in the national account relate mainly to Issyk-Kul; an old report from Naryn is given separately. Present-day local occurrence and nesting are not established.
For the species as a whole, the book describes extensive shallow salt lakes and hard-to-reach islands. For Kyrgyzstan, only historical vagrant records are confirmed.

The Asian houbara of Kyrgyzstan is represented by a historical account in which, under the heading Chlamydotis undulata, the local form C. undulata macqueenii (J. E. Gray, 1832) is explicitly named. An exact taxonomic check links it to the present-day species Chlamydotis macqueenii. The African C. undulata is therefore used neither for the present-day identity nor to illustrate this record. The English name Asian Houbara is confirmed by the International Fund for Houbara Conservation.

The national account describes rare sightings, mainly in the Issyk-Kul basin, including near Toru-Aygyr in 1988 and 1991. This information relates to past observations. A single bird or a small group in a field is not a count of the whole national population and does not confirm present-day nesting.

For the species, the source names open desert and semi-desert habitats, camouflage colouring, a mixed diet and a simple ground nest. The nest details are given as general biology of the species; even the book's recommendations called for local breeding sites to be searched for.

Among the adverse factors noted in 2006 were the ploughing of suitable areas, illegal shooting and poorly organised protection. The authors proposed surveying habitats and creating reserves. The historical national CR category is not presented as a present-day global assessment. Numbers in Kyrgyzstan remain unknown, and scientific review is pending.

The national account notes camouflage colouring of the body that allows the bird to blend in with open ground. A full morphological diagnosis is not given in the saved account; features of the African C. undulata have not been carried over.
A bird of open country; the book describes camouflage behaviour when disturbed. Historical sightings in the Issyk-Kul basin do not establish its present-day residence status.
According to the national account, it takes plant food, including ears of grain and berries, as well as ants, beetles, grasshoppers and small vertebrates.

The book's general description of the species: the nest is a hollow in sand or gravel under vegetation; the clutch is 3–4 mottled eggs. The package contains no evidence of a present-day breeding population in Kyrgyzstan.
Historical sightings mainly in the Issyk-Kul basin; the book gives observations near Toru-Aygyr in 1988 and 1991. Present-day finds have not been confirmed.
Takyr deserts, semi-deserts and desertified foothills; the book also reports autumn and winter sightings on cereal stubble.

The slender-billed curlew is a distinct species of wader that is the subject of a historical account in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. Its scientific name Numenius tenuirostris and its species rank are confirmed by an exact saved GBIF record. Its historical inclusion remains a documented fact regardless of later changes in the status of the species.

Two different assessment dates must be distinguished here. The 2006 book treated the bird as an extremely rare vagrant curlew and allowed for future sightings. However, in its final Red List update of 10 October 2025, BirdLife International confirmed the global extinction of the species. The old assumptions about future vagrant visits are therefore not used as a present-day recommendation or as evidence of an existing population.

The national account linked historical reports to the Issyk-Kul basin; the possibility of sightings in the Chüy Valley was put forward only tentatively. These levels of evidence are kept separate. The account itself gave no national population figure and noted that the country lies outside the usual migration routes.

Historical threats included shooting and the draining of suitable sites. The recommendations of the time concerned the protection of resting and feeding sites and the scientific documentation of reports. The record is now above all of historical and educational value. The national CR category field is accompanied by the year 2006, and the current report of extinction is given separately. The unknown national population size has not been replaced with an invented count, and the photograph of a museum specimen is not presented as a living present-day bird.

The 2008 RSPB/AEWA identification guide describes a slender bill with a pointed tip, dark grey legs and a white tail with a few dark bars. Identification is difficult and requires a combination of features; the guide is used for morphology, not as current evidence that the species exists.

In the 2006 source, a vagrant to Kyrgyzstan outside the usual migration routes. In 2025 BirdLife confirmed its global extinction; the description of its former behaviour does not imply present-day occurrence.

The book's historical records relate to the Issyk-Kul basin; the Chüy Valley is mentioned as a possibility, without an equally confirmed find. Present-day occurrence is not claimed; BirdLife 2025 confirmed global extinction.
The historical national account gives wetlands of the plains and the low and middle mountains as possible stopover sites for vagrant birds.

The great black-headed gull is a large gull represented in the 2006 national account under the historical spelling Larus ichtyaetus. The earlier taxonomic block was lifted during the inventory by a documentary check: the government resolution has Larus ichthyaetus, the author Pallas, 1773 matches, and the saved exact GBIF responses link the synonym to Ichthyaetus ichthyaetus. This resolution is based on sources, not on the similarity of strings.

The national account gives observations in the Chüy Valley and the Issyk-Kul basin and interprets a sighting of young birds on Son-Kul as evidence of nesting. The latter is kept specifically as a conclusion of the authors of the historical text, not as a newly verified colony. The numbers of birds on individual routes and in the 2004 counts do not add up to a national estimate.

The book associates the species with the shores of large water bodies and describes a diet of fish and small invertebrates. The adverse impacts named include disturbance, recreational use of shorelines and the destruction of nests. The authors proposed mapping nesting sites, small protected areas and work with local people.

The NT category here refers to the 2006 book; it is not a statement of current global status. Present-day national monitoring is not included in the package, and the population remains unknown. The historical ID with the spelling ichtyaetus has been kept for continuity of research, while the scientific name in the record is given in its accepted spelling.

According to the Cornell/eBird guide, a large, powerful gull. The adult in breeding plumage has a black head, incomplete pale crescents around the eyes and a red-and-black bill tip; outside the breeding season the dark colouring of the head is partly retained. Young birds look different, so a photograph of a young bird does not illustrate breeding plumage.
According to the book, it occurs singly and in small flocks, especially during migration, and prefers large water bodies. Historical observations do not replace a present-day count.
The national account names fish, small crustaceans and beetles; it also notes the stealing of food from other birds.
The 2006 book treats observations of young birds on Son-Kul as an indication of nesting. A specific present-day colony, breeding dates and breeding success are not confirmed in the package.
Historical observations: the Chüy Valley, the Issyk-Kul basin and Son-Kul; Chatyr-Kul is mentioned separately in 1972. The present-day state of local populations has not been studied.
Shores of lakes and other large water bodies, less often rivers; historical national source from 2006.

The great spotted woodpecker is a distinct, widespread species of forest bird that is the subject of a 2006 national account. The exact name Dendrocopos major is confirmed by a saved taxonomic record. The book mentions the local form brevirostris, but this record keeps the species rank of the historical heading and does not create an additional subspecies entry.

The most significant limitation of the national information is the age and small number of records. The account gives collection specimens from the Teskey Ala-Too and the Kyrgyz Range; one find is dated 1876. Material from the Tekes relates to Kazakhstan and does not become Kyrgyz merely because the regions are neighbours. The English summary explicitly calls its residence status unclear.

The book links its possible occurrence to spruce and walnut-fruit forests and describes a mainly insectivorous diet. Details of present-day breeding, numbers and specific limiting factors for the country have not been established. The RSPB's general description of the species' appearance is not used to transfer British population figures and statuses to Kyrgyzstan.

The historical recommendations concern conserving forests, preventing uncontrolled felling and restoring habitats. The NT category refers to the 2006 book. This record documents the historical national listing and does not claim the existence of a confirmed present-day local population.

According to the RSPB, the plumage is contrasting black and white with a red patch on the underparts. The male has a red spot on the nape, and young birds have a red cap. These are features of the species in general, not a diagnosis of the local subspecies brevirostris.
In the historical account, a forest bird whose national residence status is unclear. Published old collection finds do not prove a present-day resident population.
According to the national account, it feeds mainly on insects, including insects on forest trees.

The national account gives old specimens from the Teskey Ala-Too and the Kyrgyz Range; possible occurrence in the eastern Issyk-Kul area requires confirmation. Kazakh specimens from the Tekes valley are kept separate from the Kyrgyz information.
According to the 2006 book, spruce and walnut-fruit forests; occurrence in the eastern Issyk-Kul area is described as possible, not as confirmed by a present-day survey.

The Issyk-Kul marinka is a historical lake concept, named in the national book as Schizothorax issykkuli Berg. Eschmeyer’s Catalog links the type series from Issyk-Kul to the accepted Schizothorax pseudoaksaiensis Herzenstein, 1889. The species name is used with the explicit restriction that the national data refer to this local form, not to all populations of the accepted species.

The national description emphasises very small scales that do not form regular rows, and the character of the serration on the dorsal spine. Freshened shore areas of Issyk-Kul near river mouths; the 2006 national description. The book describes a seasonal move from the shallows into deeper water and the absence of large shoals. This information is not extrapolated to river populations beyond the historical account.

The historical source reports plant and animal food, including molluscs and stoneworts; fish have been recorded in the diet of large individuals. In the national account spawning is linked to the spring–summer period and to stony substrates. Detailed percentages of spawning forms and fecundity are not used as a present-day estimate.

The national data concern the shores of Issyk-Kul and the lower reaches of its tributaries. Eschmeyer’s type material is tied to the lake; no new present-day points have been created.

In 2006 the threats named were deteriorating natural reproduction, fishing and poaching, and the introduction of predatory fish. The historical recommendations were restrictions on fishing, protection of spawning sites and research into artificial breeding.

The national EN category relates to the historical 2006 account and the named local conservation unit. It is neither a global assessment of the entire modern taxon nor a verified current legal status. Present-day numbers are unknown; independent scientific verification is pending.

Freshened shore areas of Issyk-Kul near river mouths; the 2006 national description.

The Issyk-Kul scaleless osman is a lake form listed in the 2006 book as Diptychus dybowskii lansdelli Günther. Eschmeyer traces the original name Diptychus lansdelli Günther, 1889, the Issyk-Kul syntypes and its synonymy with Gymnodiptychus dybowskii (Kessler, 1874). The present-day species card restricts the national data to the historical lake conservation unit.

According to the book, the body is largely naked, with scales retained only on limited areas. There are dark spots on a silvery or golden background; the body is moderately compressed laterally. Shallows and areas where tributaries enter Issyk-Kul; a historical description from the national account. The source distinguishes between the diet of young and adult fish. No new assessment of the status of the lake form and no comparison with river populations have been carried out.

According to the national account, young fish feed on algae and zooplankton, and adults mainly on bottom-dwelling invertebrates, including molluscs and crustaceans. The book describes batch spawning on shallow spawning grounds. The spawning months differ between the RU and EN versions, so no agreed precise calendar has been assigned.

The historical coverage is the northern, western and southern parts of Issyk-Kul and the rivers flowing into it. It is not replaced by the general range of Gymnodiptychus dybowskii.

According to the 2006 source: unsustainable fishing, deterioration of spawning grounds and late maturation; the impact of introduced predators was noted as a possibility. In 2006 the recommendations were to restore artificial breeding, restrict fishing and protect spawning sites.

The national CR category relates to the historical 2006 account and the named local conservation unit. It is neither a global assessment of the entire modern taxon nor a verified current legal status. Present-day numbers are unknown; independent scientific verification is pending.

The dwarf sand boa is the historical national concept of Eryx tataricus (Lichtenstein, 1823), which the present-day treatment adopted here includes in Eryx miliaris (Pallas, 1773). The Reptile Database documents a formal synonymisation, not merely a similarity of names. The national data for the Tien Shan–Turanian concept are not automatically transferred to all populations of the broader species.

Clay, loess and gravelly desert-steppe areas on plains and in foothills; as described in the historical account. According to the book, it is active mainly at dusk and at night, using burrows and cavities under stones and roots. Its secretive habits already made it difficult to estimate numbers when the national source was being prepared.

The national account lists small reptiles and mammals, and less often birds and insects; prey is held in the coils of the body. The 2006 source describes the national concept as ovoviviparous, with mating in spring and young appearing in summer and early autumn. No new dates have been established.

The historical account names the Chüy and Talas valleys, the Ketmen-Töbö Basin and the north-east of Batken Region. This information does not confirm that every population survives today.

Historically, ploughing, intensive grazing and direct killing were recorded; commercial collection was identified as a possible factor. The 2006 recommendations included awareness-raising and restrictions on commercial collection.

The national NT category relates to the historical 2006 account and the named local conservation unit. It is neither a global assessment of the entire modern taxon nor a verified current legal status. Present-day numbers are unknown; independent scientific verification is pending.

The paradise flycatcher in the national account belongs to the explicitly named local subspecies Terpsiphone paradisi leucogaster (Swainson, 1838). The OSME 2025 regional list keeps it within Terpsiphone paradisi and associates it with western Kyrgyzstan. The old, broad Asian paradisi complex is not used in place of this specific subspecies.

Broadleaved woodland and gardens near water bodies and mountain rivers, according to the national account. The book describes the bird as tied to suitable woodland and garden habitats. A qualitative statement that it is common in particular habitats is not the same as known numbers for the country.

The historical account gives an extended breeding period and a small clutch. Present-day national productivity and breeding dates have not been separately confirmed.

The book gives the Western Tien Shan; possible sites on other ranges are retained as a supposition of the source. OSME confirms the regional use of leucogaster without providing a present-day national count.

In 2006 research into the range, numbers and conservation status was recommended; the specific limiting factors were stated to be unknown.

Broadleaved woodland and gardens near water bodies and mountain rivers, according to the national account.

Otonycteris leucophaea is a large, pale bat historically included in the national book as Otonycteris hemprichi (Peters, 1859). In the accepted present-day regional treatment by the Zoological Museum of Moscow State University, the Kyrgyz concept belongs to the separated Otonycteris leucophaea (Severtzov, 1873). Correcting the name does not mean that the old specimens have been re-examined or that a present-day population has been confirmed.

The identification guide of the Zoological Museum of Moscow State University describes a large, pale-coloured member of the vesper bats with very long ears that are not joined to each other. Semi-desert foothills with rock outcrops and scattered pistachio trees; historical information from the national book. The book describes activity at dusk and at night, a low searching flight and the capture of prey on the ground. Rock crevices and other cavities serve as roosts.

Historical diet analysis included solifuges, scorpions, spiders and insects. The percentages of individual groups from a local sample are not presented as the constant diet of all populations. The source describes breeding in Kyrgyzstan as poorly studied; the start of the season is given tentatively. Exact dates are not presented as an established present-day fact.

The book gives a historical record from 1966 near Tash-Kumyr and captures in 1992 in Aravan District. These are dated records, not present-day points or an estimate of numbers for the country.

The source supposes that animals settling near people are killed and that roosts are disturbed; no dedicated present-day assessment has been carried out. The measures recommended in 2006 were protection of roosts, small reserves and awareness-raising.

The national category, retained exactly as given in the edition, relates to the historical 2006 account and the named local conservation unit. It is neither a global assessment of the entire modern taxon nor a verified current legal status. Present-day numbers are unknown; independent scientific verification is pending.

The Tien Shan maral (wapiti) is a historical national conservation unit described as Cervus elaphus asiaticus Lydekker, 1898. The accepted MDD species standard links the name asiaticus to Cervus canadensis Erxleben, 1777. This treatment follows that name link without declaring asiaticus a separately accepted present-day subspecies.

Spruce forests and mountain scrub; the book describes seasonal movements up to subalpine meadows. According to the historical national account, wapiti are capable of seasonal movements, including across national borders. Local herds and occasional crossings are not combined into a fictitious present-day population.

The national account describes the main food as herbaceous vegetation; present-day seasonal proportions of food items have not been established. The book describes an autumn rut and young appearing in late spring to early summer. Discrepancies in some dates between RU and EN have not been used to build a precise calendar.

The national account gives Naryn-Too and the eastern Issyk-Kul area, and for some old sites explicitly notes the absence of information. The card does not carry the historical state of these places over into the present.

The historical source names felling, intensive grazing, disturbance, poaching and the limited extent of winter feeding grounds. The 2006 recommendations were protection and expansion of habitats, ecological corridors and control of poaching.

The national EN category relates to the historical 2006 account and the named local conservation unit. It is neither a global assessment of the entire modern taxon nor a verified current legal status. Present-day numbers are unknown; independent scientific verification is pending.

The Siberian jerboa is the national historical concept of Allactaga saltator Eversmann, 1848. MDD includes the original name and the names of the local forms altorum and dementiewi in a single species, Orientallactaga sibirica (J.R.Forster, 1778). The two historical forms do not produce two separate cards and are not mixed up with the already published Allactaga elater and A. severtzovi.

Clay and in places gravelly desert and semi-desert areas with sparse vegetation; historical information from the book. The national account describes a nocturnal way of life and winter hibernation. Differences in seasonal activity between sites at different altitudes have not been turned into universal exact dates.

The source lists leaves, seeds, bulbs, rhizomes and tubers; insects are recorded in small quantities. In the historical account breeding is associated with late spring and early summer. Embryo data from old observations are not an estimate of present-day fecundity for the country.

The book distinguishes two isolated local forms. Their exact distribution is not repeated as present-day: the type-locality link of the name altorum in MDD needs to be checked separately against the distribution given in the book.

The historical account lists weather conditions and predators; the material used contains no confirmed present-day assessment of human-caused threats. The 2006 book recommends conserving the habitats of the historical local forms.

The national NT category relates to the historical 2006 account and the named local conservation unit. It is neither a global assessment of the entire modern taxon nor a verified current legal status. Present-day numbers are unknown; independent scientific verification is pending.

Olga’s sorbaria is the historical name of a local shrub that has its own account in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. For this educational card the present-day species Sorbaria tomentosa has been chosen: the 2021 revision by Song and Hong explicitly treats Sorbaria olgae Zinserling as one of its synonyms, and POWO specifies the nominate variety tomentosa. This is therefore not a new identification based on a similar name, but a documented taxonomic transfer. The conservation information in the local account cannot automatically be extended to the whole present-day species.

The national description of the local form notes glabrous branches and imparipinnate leaves with 15–19 ovate-lanceolate leaflets. Their margins are doubly toothed, and the underside has scattered simple hairs along the veins. A branched inflorescence system is described. These features are summarised for the historical olgae material, not as an exhaustive diagnosis of all varieties of Sorbaria tomentosa. Gorge slopes on the northern side of the Alay Range, near Shakhimardan; the historical location given in the 2006 national account. The shrub life form is confirmed by the national description. The Russian account gives no detailed ecological requirements or information on cultivation; the English version’s suggestion about the role of grazing is not accepted as an established threat.

The national source gives flowering in May and fruiting in July. Other aspects of reproduction are described as unstudied; successful present-day reproduction of the local population is not claimed.

The book reports a find in 1871 near Shakhimardan and unsuccessful later searches. This is the state of knowledge as of 2006, not proof of present-day extinction or of a living population. The Fergana type cited in the 2021 revision is not declared a new record in Kyrgyzstan.

The 2006 account recommended repeat surveys of the historical area and the establishment of a protected site if the plant is found. The references to protection in 1975 and 1985 are historical information.

The national category relates to the local historical conservation unit described in 2006. It is not a global assessment of the entire accepted taxon, a current IUCN category or a verified legal status for 2026. Present-day national numbers remain unknown; independent scientific verification is pending.

Gorge slopes on the northern side of the Alay Range, near Shakhimardan; the historical location given in the 2006 national account.

The microcarpous dorema is included in the 2006 national book under the name Dorema microcarpum Korovin. The present-day accepted name for this card is Ferula namanganica Sennikov. POWO indicates the homotypic link between the names, and the molecular study by Puchałka and co-authors in 2023 treats this material within Ferula. The exact Catalogue of Life species key presented in GBIF has been chosen; the name Ferula microcarpum from a different backbone response has not been substituted automatically.

According to the national account, this is a tap-rooted perennial with a single stem up to 1–1.5 m tall. The basal leaves are repeatedly divided, while the stem leaves are much reduced. The umbellate Tianschaniella is a perennial plant of the Central Tien Shan, treated in the 2006 book of Kyrgyzstan under the spelling Tianschaniella umbellifera. Here Tianschaniella umbellulifera B.Fedtsch. ex Popov is accepted. The basis for the change is the 2015 typification by Ovchinnikova and the 2017 WWF regional table, which explicitly links the correct name to the national book. The alternative homotypic combination Lappula umbellulifera is not an additional species for the catalogue.

The national account describes slender ascending stems 30–40 cm tall, rosettes of basal leaves and appressed-hairy stem leaves. Clusters of flower stalks form a false umbel-like inflorescence. The corolla is bluish or whitish; the fruit splits into nutlets with winged margins and anchor-shaped prickles. Thin patches of fine soil among rocks along riverbanks and in gorges of the upper mountain belt; national information from 2006. The source describes the plant growing as single individuals or in small groups. This does not establish a quantitative estimate of the size of present-day populations. The information on flowering differs between the language versions of the book; these differences have not been corrected by guesswork.

The 2006 national account is devoted to the Tashkoroo apollo, named Parnassius loxias tashkorensis Kreuzberg, 1984. This card applies decision No. 25.8: the present-day treatment by Huang 2023 assigns tashkorensis to the nominate subspecies Parnassius loxias loxias. Subspecies rank is therefore retained; the parent species is not substituted for the local conservation unit. A museum catalogue in Kyiv independently documents a paratype from Uch-Chat in the Kaindy Range.

In the description of the local form, white wing colouring predominates; the forewings have dark transverse markings and the hindwings small red spots with a thin black rim. A translucent border runs along the outer edge. The forewing length is given as 33–35 mm; this describes the historical material, not the size of the whole present-day population. Steep, dry, eroded clay-and-stone slopes with the food plant in the middle mountain belt, at altitudes of 2500–3100 m according to the national account. In the book the larvae are associated with Krasnov’s corydalis, Corydalis krasnovi. They are active at night and hide under stones during the day; the adults feed on nectar. The isolation of the sites and the close tie to the food plant limit the dispersal of the local form.

The national source names the leaves of Corydalis krasnovi as caterpillar food; for adults it gives visits to the flowers of wild onions and members of the daisy family. These observations are not generalised to all subspecies of Parnassius loxias. According to the book there is one generation a year. The first-instar caterpillar overwinters inside the egg shell; females lay their eggs on stones next to the food plants. Historically the flight period was recorded from mid-June to mid-August.

The historical localities of the Tashkoroo form are given in the basin of the left-bank tributaries of the Sary-Jaz, at the western ends of Kaindy-Katta and Inylchek-Too. Present-day synonymy with the nominate subspecies does not turn all its localities abroad into national ones. No new survey of these populations is claimed.

In 2006 micro-reserves, monitoring of reproduction and regulation of pressure on the vegetation were proposed. Artificial expansion of the range remains a proposal of that source, not a measure that has been carried out.

Merzbacher’s apollo butterfly is a subspecies of Parnassius apollo with its own national account in 2006. This treatment accepts Parnassius apollo merzbacheri following Huang 2023: the author explicitly recognises the subspecies and lists chryseis among its synonyms. The exact subspecies record of ENA taxonomy in GBIF is consistent with this scope. The synonym backbone key leading to the parent apollo is not used as the accepted subspecies identifier.

The white or creamy wings bear a black pattern; on each hindwing there are two conspicuous red spots with black rims and more or less distinct pale centres. According to the book, males are usually paler and smaller than females. The numerical wingspan differs between the language versions of the account and is not standardised here. Mid-mountain meadow-forest and meadow-steppe landscapes, and stony slopes with tall-herb and subalpine meadows at altitudes of 1000–3000 m; a historical description of the local form. The dhole, or Cuon alpinus, is a separate species of the dog family included in the 2006 Red Data Book of Kyrgyzstan. The old account doubted the identification of six skins received in 1922–1956. This treatment takes into account an independent type specimen, ZIN No. 23894, from At-Bashy in 1907 and a genetic find published by Cancellare and co-authors in 2022. These new grounds do not declare the disputed skins to have been correctly identified.

According to the historical national description, steppe-like parts of the alpine and subalpine belts and the upper part of the forest belt, associated with places where wild ungulates concentrate. The species is social; the national account describes it forming packs and being active both by day and by night. A single genetic find does not prove the presence of a stable local pack or a breeding population in 2026.

The national source names wild ungulates, including ibex, as its prey. This describes the species’ diet as given in the account, not a quantitatively established diet of the present Kyrgyz population. The book gives a winter breeding season and the birth of several pups for the species. This general biological information does not mean that breeding has been confirmed in the wild in Kyrgyzstan today.

In a scat sample collected on 15 August 2019 in southern Kyrgyzstan, a 2021 analysis identified a 147 bp fragment of mitochondrial cytb as Cuon alpinus. The result was published in 2022 and deposited as GenBank MZ813093. Present-day numbers, the regularity of its presence and reproduction in this area have not been established.

The 2006 book recommends searching for reliable records and subsequent monitoring. The 2022 study justifies further monitoring but does not confirm that a population recovery programme has been carried out.
